# Technology Stack Selection with Next.js, Supabase, and Claude API

Recommended stack: Next.js 14+ App Router frontend, Supabase PostgreSQL database, Anthropic Claude API via Vercel AI SDK.

The second thought in the sequential analysis process evaluated and selected the technology stack for transfo-ia-okr. For the frontend, Next.js 14+ with App Router was chosen over Vue/Nuxt and SvelteKit, offering server-side rendering for performance and SEO, React Server Components, built-in API routes, excellent TypeScript support, and access to the large React ecosystem including shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS. The backend architecture takes a pragmatic MVP-first approach using Next.js API Routes rather than a separate Node.js/Express or Python FastAPI server, reducing initial complexity while maintaining the ability to extract services later as scalability demands increase. For the database, Supabase was selected over raw PostgreSQL or MongoDB because it provides PostgreSQL's relational strengths (essential for OKR hierarchies and relationships) while including built-in authentication and realtime capabilities that reduce boilerplate code. The AI integration strategy selected Anthropic's Claude API accessed via Vercel AI SDK, prioritizing Claude's superior reasoning capabilities for OKR analysis and suggestions over OpenAI alternatives or local LLM deployment. This stack balances modern development practices, MVP velocity, and future scalability while leveraging integrated platforms (Supabase, Vercel) to minimize infrastructure complexity during Phase 0.

# Next.js App Router Authentication Patterns Retrieved from Documentation

Context7 MCP provided authentication patterns including session management, password hashing, middleware protection, and role-based authorization.

The context7 MCP server was invoked to retrieve Next.js App Router authentication patterns and enterprise application architecture guidance from official documentation. The query returned five comprehensive authentication patterns essential for secure application architecture. The signup action demonstrates form validation followed by bcrypt password hashing (10 rounds) and database insertion using Drizzle ORM, with proper error handling for duplicate users. Session management shows a secure pattern of creating database sessions with 7-day expiration, encrypting session IDs, and storing them in HTTP-only cookies with secure flags (httpOnly, secure, sameSite: lax). Route handler security implements a two-tier authorization system: first verifying session existence (returning 401 for unauthenticated users), then validating role permissions (returning 403 for insufficient privileges). The middleware proxy pattern enables optimistic authentication checks by reading and decrypting session cookies, automatically redirecting unauthenticated users from protected routes to login and authenticated users from public routes to dashboard. The middleware configuration includes a matcher that excludes API routes, Next.js static assets, and image files from authentication processing, optimizing performance. These patterns provide production-ready authentication architecture aligned with Next.js 14+ App Router best practices, supporting the technical stack decisions made in the previous sequential thinking step.

# OKR Domain Model Data Architecture Defined

Designed comprehensive entity-relationship model with 8 core entities supporting multi-tenancy, hierarchical teams, and cascading OKRs.

The data model architecture was designed using sequential-thinking MCP to define the core domain entities for the OKR management platform. The model follows a hierarchical structure starting with Organization as the multi-tenancy root, containing Teams that can nest via parent_team_id. This design supports key OKR platform requirements including cascading goals, weighted KR scoring, hierarchical team structures, and multi-tenancy isolation.

# Supabase Row Level Security Implementation Patterns

Context7 MCP query retrieved comprehensive RLS policy patterns for authentication, user data isolation, and automated profile creation triggers.

The Context7 MCP server query retrieved comprehensive documentation on Supabase Row Level Security (RLS) implementation patterns for database security and authentication integration. RLS policies control data access at the PostgreSQL row level, enabling user data isolation and fine-grained permissions. The fundamental pattern uses auth.uid() to match the authenticated user's ID against ownership columns (user_id, author_id). Policies are optimized by targeting specific roles (TO authenticated) to prevent unnecessary evaluation for anonymous sessions. Different policy operations (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) enable granular control: public read policies use USING (true) for authenticated users while write policies enforce owner checks with WITH CHECK clauses. Advanced patterns support multi-party access scenarios like ride-sharing apps where both driver and passenger can access the same ride record. The documentation includes a complete example with profiles and posts tables demonstrating public viewability, owner-only modifications, and automated profile creation using PostgreSQL triggers that fire on auth.users inserts, extracting metadata fields to populate the profiles table. This RLS architecture provides database-level security without relying solely on application-layer access control.

Faits: ["Row Level Security enabled via ALTER TABLE table_name ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY command in PostgreSQL","Basic user isolation policy uses auth.uid() = user_id pattern to restrict users to their own data","Policy optimization targets 'authenticated' role with TO authenticated clause to prevent unnecessary execution for anonymous users","Multiple policy types support different operations: FOR SELECT (read), FOR INSERT (create), FOR UPDATE (modify), FOR DELETE (remove)","Public read patterns use USING (true) to allow all authenticated users to view data while restricting modifications to owners","Automated profile creation uses trigger function handle_new_user() on auth.users table to create profiles entry with raw_user_meta_data fields on signup","Complex access patterns combine auth.uid() checks with business logic like driver_id = auth.uid() OR passenger_id = auth.uid() for multi-party access"]
summary: Supabase Row Level Security Implementation Patterns

# AI Capabilities Defined with Claude API and Vercel AI SDK Integration

Four core AI features planned: OKR Assistant, Progress Analysis, Alignment Analysis, and Retrospective Insights with server-side implementation.

The fifth sequential thinking step defined comprehensive AI capabilities that differentiate transfo-ia-okr as an AI-powered OKR platform. Four core AI features were designed: OKR Assistant provides proactive guidance by suggesting objectives based on company context, generating aligned key results, recommending appropriate metrics and targets, and identifying potential conflicts between OKRs across teams. Progress Analysis uses predictive analytics to analyze check-in patterns, forecast goal achievement likelihood, flag at-risk key results based on current trajectory, and suggest corrective actions before cycles end. Alignment Analysis ensures strategic coherence by checking team OKR alignment with company-level objectives, detecting gaps in strategic coverage, and recommending cascading relationships to improve organizational alignment. Retrospective Insights mines historical data from completed OKR cycles to identify success patterns and blockers, generating actionable improvement recommendations for future cycles. The technical implementation leverages Vercel AI SDK for streaming responses paired with Anthropic Claude API for superior reasoning capabilities on these complex strategic tasks. A server-side only architecture via Next.js API routes ensures security and cost control by preventing direct client access to AI APIs. The design starts with simple prompt-based approaches but includes RAG pattern capability (embedding OKR context) for evolution if needed. Cost control mechanisms include per-user daily AI request limits, caching common suggestions to reduce API calls, and background processing for batch analysis tasks. The architecture explicitly rejects local LLM deployment as overkill for MVP and fine-tuning as unnecessary given Claude's out-of-box reasoning capabilities.

Comprehensive architecture document defining Next.js fullstack, Supabase backend, Prisma ORM, and AI integration for OKR platform.

The technical architecture document was created defining the complete technology stack and design decisions for the transfo-ia-okr OKR management platform. The architecture follows a monolithic-first approach using Next.js 14+ fullstack framework with App Router, React Server Components, and Server Actions for the presentation layer. The UI layer combines shadcn/ui (Radix-based accessible components), Tailwind CSS v4 for styling, Tremor for data visualization, and React Hook Form with Zod for type-safe form validation. The backend leverages Next.js API Routes for serverless endpoints, Supabase as Backend-as-a-Service providing PostgreSQL database with native Row Level Security, authentication with OAuth (Google/Microsoft), realtime WebSocket subscriptions, and file storage. Prisma ORM v5+ handles type-safe database access and migrations. AI capabilities are integrated via Anthropic Claude API through Vercel AI SDK, enabling five core features: OKR Assistant for suggestions, Progress Analysis for trajectory prediction, Risk Detection for at-risk KRs, Alignment Check for strategic validation, and Retrospective Insights for historical analysis. Cost control is implemented with daily user limits, response caching, batch processing, and claude-3-haiku for simple tasks. The data model implements an 8-entity schema supporting multi-tenancy (Organization root), hierarchical teams (parent_id), cascading objectives (parent_objective_id), flexible metrics (percentage/number/currency/boolean), weighted KR scoring, initiatives tracking, progress check-ins with confidence levels, and polymorphic comments. Security is enforced through RLS policies isolating organizations, JWT sessions with refresh tokens, Next.js auth middleware, and server-side Zod validation. Four ADRs justify key decisions: Next.js for RSC/Server Actions/TypeScript, Supabase for integrated PostgreSQL/Auth/Realtime, monolithic architecture for MVP simplicity, and Claude API for superior reasoning. The project structure organizes code into app router directories ((auth), (dashboard)), component layers (ui, objectives, charts, layout, providers), lib utilities (supabase, ai, utils, validations), type definitions, Prisma schema, and test folders. # Complete Prisma Schema Implemented for OKR Data Model

Created 8-model database schema with hierarchical relationships, cascade deletes, and composite indexes matching architecture specification.

The complete Prisma schema was implemented replacing the default template with the full OKR data model defined in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md. The schema configures prisma-client-js generator and PostgreSQL datasource with dual connection strings (DATABASE_URL for connection pooling, DIRECT_URL for migrations) for Supabase compatibility. The 8-model structure implements multi-tenant architecture starting with Organization as the root entity containing teams, users, and objectives. Team supports hierarchical nesting through a self-referential TeamHierarchy relation via parentId. User belongs to Organization and participates in multiple teams through the TeamMember junction table (composite key: teamId + userId). The OKR hierarchy flows from Objective (with optional team assignment and parent-child cascading via ObjectiveHierarchy relation) to KeyResult (flexible metric types: percentage/number/currency/boolean with start/target/current values and weight for scoring) to Initiative (actionable tasks with status and priority tracking). Supporting models include CheckIn for progress updates with confidence levels (1-10 scale) and Comment using a polymorphic pattern (entityType + entityId) with composite index optimization. All foreign keys implement onDelete: Cascade for automatic cleanup except strategic references (team assignments, ownership) to prevent accidental data loss. Field naming follows snake_case database conventions using @map directives while maintaining camelCase in Prisma Client. This schema enables the complete OKR management workflow with organizational isolation, hierarchical teams, cascading objectives, weighted key results, and collaborative features.

# Supabase Middleware Session Handler Implemented

Created middleware utility to refresh Supabase authentication sessions using cookie-based storage for Next.js server-side requests.

Created a Supabase middleware session handler in src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts to manage authentication state in Next.js server-side contexts. The updateSession function creates a server-side Supabase client using the @supabase/ssr package's createServerClient method, configured with environment variables for the Supabase project URL and anonymous API key. The implementation handles cookie-based session management through a custom cookies adapter: the getAll() method reads all cookies from the incoming NextRequest, and setAll() propagates cookie updates to both the request and response objects, ensuring session tokens are properly maintained across middleware execution. The function calls supabase.auth.getUser() which triggers automatic session refresh if the current token has expired, obtaining a new access token using the refresh token stored in cookies. This middleware pattern enables seamless authentication persistence across server components, API routes, and middleware without requiring explicit token management in application code. The function returns the modified NextResponse with updated authentication cookies, allowing protected routes and server-side data fetching to access valid user sessions.

# Prisma Client Singleton Pattern Implemented

Created global Prisma client instance with development-mode caching to prevent connection exhaustion during hot reloading.

The Prisma client singleton was implemented in src/lib/prisma.ts to manage database connections efficiently across the Next.js application. The pattern uses a global variable cached in globalThis to store the PrismaClient instance during development, preventing connection pool exhaustion caused by Next.js hot module replacement creating multiple client instances on file changes. In production (NODE_ENV === 'production'), the global caching is skipped and a fresh PrismaClient is instantiated, ensuring proper resource cleanup and avoiding potential memory leaks in deployed environments. The implementation uses TypeScript type assertions to safely extend globalThis with an optional prisma property typed as PrismaClient | undefined. The nullish coalescing operator (??) checks if a global instance exists before creating a new one. This singleton pattern is a Next.js best practice for Prisma integration, ensuring a single client manages the connection pool across server components, API routes, and server actions. # GitHub Actions CI Pipeline Configured

Three-job CI workflow created for lint, test, and build verification on main/develop branches with Node.js 20.

A GitHub Actions CI pipeline was configured in .github/workflows/ci.yml implementing a three-stage validation workflow for code quality, testing, and build verification. The pipeline triggers on push and pull_request events targeting main and develop branches, running on ubuntu-latest with Node.js 20. The workflow orchestrates three parallel-then-sequential jobs: the Lint job validates code quality by running ESLint and TypeScript type checking independently; the Test job executes the test suite (Vitest) in parallel with linting; and the Build job runs only after both lint and test jobs succeed, ensuring broken code never reaches the build stage. All jobs use modern GitHub Actions (checkout@v4, setup-node@v4) with npm caching to optimize installation speed. The jobs use npm ci instead of npm install for deterministic, clean installations from package-lock.json, critical for reproducible CI builds. The build job includes Prisma client generation before the Next.js build since generated types are required for TypeScript compilation. Environment variables for Supabase (NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY) use GitHub secrets with fallback placeholder values allowing builds to succeed even without configured secrets. This CI configuration aligns with the architecture's emphasis on code quality gates and automated validation, implementing the GitHub Actions strategy defined in the tech stack decisions.

# Testing Library Jest-DOM Matchers Installed

@testing-library/jest-dom added as dev dependency providing custom DOM matchers for improved test assertions.

The @testing-library/jest-dom package was installed as a development dependency to enhance the Vitest testing setup with custom DOM assertion matchers. This library extends the expect() API with specialized matchers designed for testing DOM elements, providing more expressive and readable assertions than vanilla matchers. Instead of writing expect(element.classList.contains('active')).toBe(true), developers can write expect(element).toHaveClass('active'). The package includes matchers for DOM presence (toBeInTheDocument, toBeInTheDOM), visibility (toBeVisible, toBeEmptyDOMElement), form state (toBeDisabled, toBeEnabled, toBeChecked), text content (toHaveTextContent, toContainElement), styling (toHaveClass, toHaveStyle), accessibility (toHaveAccessibleName, toHaveAccessibleDescription), and more. The installation brought in 9 additional packages, likely including peer dependencies and type definitions, bringing the total audited package count to 592. The build completed successfully in 4 seconds, though npm audit flagged 7 moderate severity vulnerabilities in the dependency tree, suggesting npm audit fix for patches that won't introduce breaking changes. These vulnerabilities are likely in transitive dependencies and should be addressed but don't block development. The package will be imported in src/test/setup.ts (referenced in vitest.config.ts) to globally extend Vitest's expect matchers.

# Prisma Schema Defines Complete OKR Domain Model with Hierarchical Structure

Database schema models organizations, teams, objectives, key results, initiatives, check-ins, and comments with full relationship mapping.

The Prisma schema implements a comprehensive OKR (Objectives and Key Results) domain model for the transfo-ia-okr platform using PostgreSQL. The data architecture supports multi-tenant organizations with hierarchical team structures, where teams can have parent-child relationships enabling organizational depth. Objectives can cascade through the hierarchy with parent-child links, allowing alignment from company-wide goals down to team-specific targets. Each objective contains multiple key results that track quantifiable progress using various metric types (percentage, numeric, currency, boolean) with start, target, and current values. Initiatives break down key results into concrete action items with status tracking and priority levels. The check-in model enables regular progress updates with confidence scoring, while a flexible comment system supports discussions on any entity type. User management spans organization and team membership with role-based access control. The schema enforces data integrity through cascade deletion rules and proper foreign key constraints, ensuring consistent state when entities are removed.

Faits: ["Schema defines 10 models: Organization, Team, User, TeamMember, Objective, KeyResult, Initiative, CheckIn, and Comment","Hierarchical structures support nested teams (parent-child via TeamHierarchy relation) and cascading objectives (ObjectiveHierarchy relation)","Key results track metrics with metricType (percentage, number, currency, boolean), startValue, targetValue, currentValue, and optional unit field","User roles defined at organization level (admin, manager, member) and team level (lead, member) for permission management","Check-ins store progress updates with value, note, and confidence score (1-10 scale) linked to key results","Initiatives represent actionable tasks with status (todo, in_progress, done), priority levels (low, medium, high, critical), and due dates","Comments system supports polymorphic relationships via entityType and entityId fields for objectives, key results, and initiatives","All entities include cascade deletion for data integrity when parent organizations or teams are removed"]

The technology stack leverages Next.js App Router with React Server Components for performance, Supabase for backend services with built-in Row Level Security, Prisma as the type-safe ORM layer, and Claude API for AI-powered features. The document includes detailed ER diagrams, complete Prisma schema definitions, project structure with folder organization, and architectural decision records justifying key technology choices. Four ADRs explain the rationale for Next.js over alternatives, Supabase as BaaS, monolithic-first architecture for simplicity, and Claude API for superior reasoning capabilities. The architecture supports the platform's core objectives of complete OKR management, organizational hierarchy with cascading objectives, real-time updates, and multi-tenant isolation.

# OAuth Callback Route Handler Implemented for Supabase Authentication

API route exchanges authorization code for session with environment-aware redirects to dashboard or custom destination.

The OAuth callback route completes the Supabase authentication flow by handling the redirect from the OAuth provider with an authorization code. When users authenticate via email magic link or OAuth providers, Supabase redirects them to this callback endpoint with a temporary code parameter. The route exchanges this code for a proper user session using Supabase's exchangeCodeForSession method, which sets the authentication cookies. The redirect logic adapts to different deployment environments: in development it uses the origin directly, in production behind proxies it checks for x-forwarded-host headers to construct HTTPS URLs, and falls back to origin for standard deployments. The next parameter allows flexible post-authentication navigation, defaulting to /dashboard but supporting custom destinations for preserving user intent. If code exchange fails or no code is provided, users are redirected back to login with an error parameter for debugging.

# Supabase Middleware Implements Route Protection and Authentication Flow

Middleware guards protected routes, redirects unauthenticated users to login, and prevents authenticated users from accessing auth pages.

The Supabase middleware was enhanced with comprehensive route protection logic implementing a complete authentication flow. The updateSession function now checks user authentication status against two route arrays: protectedRoutes requiring login and authRoutes for login/registration pages. When unauthenticated users attempt to access protected routes like /dashboard, they are redirected to /login with the original destination preserved in a redirect query parameter, enabling post-login navigation back to the intended page. Conversely, authenticated users attempting to access /login or /register are automatically redirected to /dashboard, preventing confusion and unnecessary re-authentication. The middleware uses startsWith() for route matching, allowing entire route hierarchies to be protected (e.g., /dashboard/settings). The Supabase auth client retrieves the current user session, and the middleware coordinates with Next.js cookie handling to maintain session state across requests. This pattern establishes a security boundary ensuring sensitive application areas remain inaccessible without proper authentication.

# Project Constitution v1.0.0 Established with Six Core Development Principles

Constitution defines mandatory standards for type safety, testing, security, architecture, and workflow governance.

The project constitution establishes foundational governance for the transfo-ia-okr OKR management platform with six core principles that define development standards. The User-Centric OKR Design principle prioritizes intuitive interfaces with WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility, minimal friction workflows, actionable data presentation, and responsive-first mobile experience. Type-Safe Development is marked as non-negotiable, requiring TypeScript strict mode, Prisma-generated types for all database operations, Zod validation schemas for all inputs, and justified exceptions for any explicit any types to prevent runtime errors. Test-Driven Quality mandates 80% minimum coverage for business logic since OKR calculations and progression metrics are critical for business decisions. The Server-First Architecture principle leverages Next.js App Router with Server Components by default, using Client Components only for interactivity, Server Actions for mutations, and API Routes for external integrations. Data Integrity & Security addresses the confidential nature of strategic OKR data by requiring Row Level Security on all Supabase tables, server-side authentication verification, strict organization data isolation, and environment-based secret management. The Simplicity & YAGNI principle guards against technical debt from unjustified complexity by prohibiting over-engineering, speculative features, and premature abstractions. The constitution documents mandatory and optional technology stack requirements, defines Git workflow with conventional commits and quality gates (lint/typecheck/test/build), integrates Ralph Loop task execution from .taskmaster/TASKS/tasks-ralph.md, and establishes governance for amendments with sync impact reports and semver versioning. This constitution provides the framework for consistent, secure, maintainable development aligned with OKR platform requirements.

# Utility Function cn() Combines clsx and tailwind-merge for Class Management

Helper merges Tailwind classes with conflict resolution using clsx for conditionals and twMerge for deduplication.

The utils.ts file provides a standard utility function cn() (short for "classnames") that combines two popular libraries for managing CSS classes in React components. The clsx library handles conditional class application, accepting strings, arrays, objects with boolean values, and nested structures. The tailwind-merge library wraps clsx output to intelligently merge Tailwind CSS classes, resolving conflicts when multiple utility classes target the same CSS property. For example, if both "px-4" and "px-6" are applied, twMerge keeps only "px-6" since it appears last. This pattern is standard in shadcn/ui components and modern React applications using Tailwind CSS, enabling clean composition of base classes with variant-specific overrides without CSS specificity issues. The function simplifies component prop APIs where consumers can pass className props that merge cleanly with component defaults.

Official patterns for sidebar navigation with nested menus, collapsible sections, and responsive mobile layouts.

The Context7 MCP server was invoked to retrieve official shadcn/ui documentation for implementing sidebar navigation components. The query targeted responsive navigation patterns and mobile menu implementations, returning five progressively complex examples from the official documentation. The examples demonstrate the component architecture: a basic sidebar with menu items and icons using SidebarMenu/SidebarMenuItem/SidebarMenuButton, nested two-level navigation using SidebarMenuSub components for hierarchical structures, dynamic rendering from project data arrays, complete layouts with SidebarInset headers containing toggle triggers, and fully collapsible menus using the Collapsible component with animated chevron indicators. The patterns show a consistent data-driven approach where menu items are defined as arrays with title, url, icon, and optional nested items, then dynamically rendered using map functions. # Sidebar Skeleton Width Changed from Random to Fixed for Deterministic Rendering

SidebarMenuSkeleton width changed from 50-90% random value to fixed 70% for consistent server-side rendering.

A bug fix was applied to the SidebarMenuSkeleton component to address a potential hydration mismatch issue in Next.js server-side rendering. The original implementation used React.useMemo with Math.random() to generate a random width between 50-90% for the skeleton loading state. While this creates visual variety, it causes hydration errors because the server-rendered HTML uses a different random value than the client-side React reconciliation. When the client hydrates the component, React detects the mismatch between server and client content, triggering console warnings and potentially causing layout shifts. The fix replaces the random width calculation with a fixed 70% value, ensuring the skeleton renders identically on both server and client. This maintains a reasonable skeleton appearance while eliminating non-deterministic behavior. The change preserves the CSS custom property pattern (--skeleton-width) for future flexibility if different skeleton widths are needed per use case.

Faits: ["src/components/ui/sidebar.tsx SidebarMenuSkeleton component modified to use fixed width instead of random width","Original implementation used React.useMemo with Math.random() generating 50-90% width values","Fixed width set to 70% for deterministic rendering behavior","Change prevents hydration mismatches in Next.js server-side rendering where random values differ between server and client","Comment updated to clarify \"Fixed width for skeleton (deterministic rendering)\" replacing \"Random width between 50 to 90%\""]

# Prisma Schema Defines Complete OKR Domain Model with 8 Entities

Database schema establishes Organization, Team, User, Objective, KeyResult, Initiative, CheckIn, and Comment models with relationships.

The Prisma schema provides a comprehensive domain model for the OKR management platform with 8 interconnected entities. At the top level, Organization serves as the multi-tenant container with all child entities configured for cascade deletion to ensure data integrity. The Team model supports hierarchical organization structures through a self-referential relationship, enabling department trees. Users are scoped to organizations with role-based access (admin, manager, member) and maintain ownership relations to objectives, key results, initiatives, check-ins, and comments. The Objective model is the core entity with period tracking (Q1 2026, H1 2026, etc.), lifecycle status transitions (draft → active → completed → archived), and optional parent/child relationships for cascading company-wide to team-specific OKRs. KeyResult entities support four metric types with configurable start/target/current values and weighted importance for calculating objective progress. Initiatives provide action item tracking linked to key results with standard task management fields (status, priority, due date). The CheckIn model enables progress tracking with value updates, explanatory notes, and confidence scoring on a 1-10 scale. Comments use a polymorphic pattern to enable discussion on any entity type. All models include created_at and updated_at timestamps for audit trails. This schema supports the complete Phase 1 feature set defined in tasks P1-03 through P1-09.

# Context7 MCP Queried for Prisma Client CRUD TypeScript Patterns

Retrieved official documentation examples showing findUnique, findMany, create, update, delete with type-safe where/data objects and relation handling.

The Context7 MCP server was queried to retrieve official Prisma documentation examples for implementing TypeScript CRUD operations with Prisma Client. The documentation reveals Prisma's structured approach to database operations using type-safe objects rather than direct parameters. All CRUD methods follow consistent patterns: where objects specify filtering criteria using unique fields (findUnique, update, delete) or complex conditions (findMany), while data objects contain the input values for mutations (create, update). Prisma supports nested operations enabling creation of related records in single transactions - for example, creating a user with posts and categories simultaneously through nested create blocks. The include clause provides eager loading of relations by specifying which related records to fetch, offering type-safe alternatives to Prisma v1's string-based fragments. The select clause enables field-level projection, reducing over-fetching by returning only specified fields. The NestJS service pattern example demonstrates production-ready service layer architecture using Prisma-generated TypeScript types for parameters: WhereUniqueInput for single-record lookups, WhereInput for filtering, OrderByWithRelationInput for sorting, and CreateInput/UpdateInput for mutations. The findMany method supports advanced querying with skip/take for offset pagination, cursor for keyset pagination, where for filtering, and orderBy for sorting. This query to Context7 likely precedes implementation of the service layer (P1-03) where these patterns will be applied to Organization, Team, User, Objective, KeyResult, and Initiative services.

# OKR Progress Calculation Engine Implemented with Risk Assessment and Trend Analysis

Comprehensive utility library calculates Key Result and Objective progress using weighted averages, risk detection, and velocity predictions.

The OKR calculations engine provides the mathematical foundation for tracking progress across the platform's objectives and key results. Key Result progress is calculated as percentage completion from start to target values, with special handling for boolean metrics and zero-range edge cases. Progress is clamped to 0-100% for display purposes, though raw progress can exceed 100% to track over-performance. Objective progress aggregates multiple Key Results using weighted averages when weights are defined, enabling strategic prioritization of certain results. The risk assessment algorithm compares actual progress against time-based expected progress - if a Key Result lags more than 20% behind where it should be based on elapsed time, it's flagged as at-risk. This provides early warning for interventions. Trend analysis examines check-in history to determine if values are moving up, down, or staying stable (within 5% threshold), while velocity calculations enable prediction of final values based on current rate of change. Formatting utilities handle internationalization with French locale number formatting, currency display in EUR, and appropriate units for different metric types. The color coding system provides visual feedback: green for on-track (70%+), yellow for caution (40-69%), and red for danger (below 40% or at-risk). Confidence tracking aggregates team member confidence levels from check-ins to surface concerns even when numbers look good. This comprehensive calculation layer ensures consistent, accurate progress reporting across all OKR views in the application.

# Prisma Client Singleton Pattern Implemented for Database Connection Management

Database client configured with environment-aware logging and hot-reload protection preventing connection exhaustion in development.

The Prisma database client was configured using the singleton pattern to solve a common Next.js development issue where hot module replacement creates multiple database connections, potentially exhausting connection pools. The implementation stores a single PrismaClient instance on the global object, checking for its existence before creating a new one using the nullish coalescing operator. This ensures the same client is reused across hot reloads during development. Logging configuration adapts to the environment: development mode enables comprehensive logging including SQL queries, errors, and warnings to aid debugging, while production restricts logging to errors only to minimize performance overhead and log volume. The singleton pattern is only applied in non-production environments because production deployments don't experience hot reload and benefit from proper instance cleanup on each deployment. This approach follows Prisma best practices for Next.js applications and aligns with the project constitution's requirement for database integrity and efficient resource usage. The module exports both named and default exports for flexible import patterns across the codebase.

# OKR Calculations Test Fixed for JavaScript Rounding Behavior

Test updated to match Math.round() behavior where 75.5 rounds to 76, not 75.

A test bug was fixed in the OKR calculations test suite where the formatMetricValue percentage formatting test had an incorrect expectation. The original test expected formatMetricValue(75.5, 'percentage') to return '75%', but JavaScript's Math.round() function rounds 75.5 to 76, not 75. This is because JavaScript implements standard mathematical rounding where values at .5 round up to the next integer. The test was corrected to expect '76%' for the 75.5 input, and an additional test case was added for 75.4 to verify it correctly rounds down to '75%'. A clarifying comment was added to document JavaScript's rounding behavior for future reference. This fix ensures the test suite accurately validates the actual behavior of the formatting utility rather than an incorrect assumption about rounding semantics.

Faits: ["src/test/okr-calculations.test.ts formatMetricValue test updated to fix incorrect expected value","Original test expected formatMetricValue(75.5, 'percentage') to return '75%' but Math.round(75.5) returns 76 in JavaScript","Test now correctly expects '76%' for 75.5 and adds additional test case for 75.4 expecting '75%'","Comment added explaining \"Math.round(75.5) = 76 en JS\" to document JavaScript's rounding behavior","JavaScript uses round-half-up (banker's rounding) where .5 rounds to nearest even or always rounds up depending on implementation"]

KeyResult and MetricType imports removed from okr-calculations.ts as they were not directly used.

The OKR calculations utility module underwent import cleanup by removing unused type imports while preserving functionality. The KeyResult and MetricType types were removed from imports because the module functions use inline object type definitions with specific properties rather than importing the full Prisma-generated types. This approach provides flexibility as functions only require the specific fields needed for calculations (startValue, targetValue, currentValue, metricType, weight) rather than entire entity types. The module contains comprehensive OKR calculation logic including key result progress calculation with boolean metric handling and division-by-zero protection, objective progress using weighted averages across key results, risk assessment comparing actual versus expected temporal progress, trend analysis from check-in histories, velocity calculation for predicting final values, and formatting helpers for displaying metrics in French locale with appropriate currency, percentage, or unit formatting. This refactoring improves code clarity by removing unused imports while maintaining all calculation capabilities essential for OKR tracking and visualization.

# P1-04 Implementation Strategy Using Server Actions Over API Routes

Architecture decision to use Next.js 15+ App Router patterns with Server Actions for mutations instead of client-side API calls.

The sequential-thinking MCP began analyzing P1-04 CRUD Objectives implementation with a multi-step reasoning process. The first thought establishes the implementation scope of 11 files and reviews satisfied dependencies including the service layer from P1-03 and dashboard layout from P1-02. A critical architectural decision emerged: following Next.js 15+ App Router patterns, the implementation will use Server Components as the default pattern with Server Actions for data mutations, rather than traditional client-side API calls. This approach aligns with modern Next.js architecture where Server Components handle data fetching server-side, and Server Actions provide a typesafe way to handle mutations without exposing API endpoints to the client. Client Components will be used selectively only for interactive elements like forms and filters. The implementation plan sequences work across 5 phases: (1) API Routes for external/programmatic access, (2) Server Actions for UI mutations, (3) Client Components for interactive UI, (4) Server Component pages with server-side data fetching, and (5) comprehensive testing. This architecture decision prioritizes server-first execution, type safety, and reduced client-side JavaScript while maintaining the interactive features needed for OKR management. The analysis identified three specialized agents for the work: frontend-architect for UI/UX patterns, backend-architect for data integrity, and quality-engineer for testing strategy.

# Objective Service Provides 20+ Functions for Complete CRUD and Progress Operations

Service layer implements read operations with multiple query patterns, write operations, progress calculations, and utility functions for P1-04 implementation.

The objective.service.ts file provides a comprehensive service layer for P1-04 CRUD Objectives implementation with 20+ exported functions organized into four logical groups. Read operations offer flexible querying: getObjectiveById for basic retrieval, getObjectiveWithKeyResults including key results, and getObjectiveWithRelations loading complete nested data (owner, team, parent, children, key results with recent check-ins and initiatives). The getObjectives function implements server-side pagination with configurable page/limit and supports multi-faceted filtering including status (single or array), period, teamId, ownerId, parentId (including null for root objectives), and full-text search across title/description fields. It returns PaginatedResponse with metadata for total count, total pages, and hasMore flag. Specialized queries getRootObjectives, getChildObjectives, getObjectivesByTeam, and getObjectivesByOwner enable hierarchy and ownership-based views. Write operations follow standard CRUD patterns: createObjective accepts CreateObjectiveInput with defaults (status='draft'), updateObjective performs partial updates with undefined checks, and deleteObjective removes records. Progress operations integrate with okr-calculations utilities: getObjectiveProgress calls getObjectiveProgressSummary with key results data and calculates weighted progress, while updateObjectiveStatus handles status transitions. Utility functions support existence checks, key result validation, and period discovery. An internal helper calculateKeyResultProgressFromValues handles progress calculation with special logic for boolean metrics (0 or 100) and range-based percentage for numeric metrics with clamping to prevent overflow. This service layer provides all backend operations needed for P1-04's API routes and Server Actions.

# Auth Callback Route Demonstrates Next.js Route Handler Patterns with URL Parsing and Redirects

Existing route shows GET handler implementation with request.url parsing, Supabase client usage, error handling, and environment-aware redirects.

The auth callback route demonstrates established Route Handler patterns used in the project. The GET function receives a Request object and extracts URL data using new URL(request.url), destructuring searchParams and origin for accessing query parameters (code, next). The Supabase client is instantiated asynchronously with await createClient(), showing the project's pattern for server-side client creation. The authentication flow calls supabase.auth.exchangeCodeForSession(code) and checks for errors using a positive success path (if !error) rather than throwing exceptions. On success, the route performs environment-aware redirects: checking process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' for local environments, inspecting x-forwarded-host header for production deployments behind proxies, with fallback to origin-based redirects. All redirects use NextResponse.redirect() with dynamically constructed URLs combining origin/host with the next parameter (defaulting to '/dashboard'). On failure, users are redirected to /login with an error query parameter. This pattern establishes conventions P1-04 should follow: async function exports, URL/searchParams parsing for query parameters, positive-path error handling (checking for success rather than catching exceptions where possible), NextResponse for responses, and environment-aware logic. The import pattern from '@/lib/supabase/server' using path aliases shows project conventions. Unlike the callback route which uses GET for redirects, P1-04's API routes will return JSON responses using Response.json() or NextResponse.json() for CRUD operations with appropriate HTTP status codes.

# Supabase Server Client Uses Async Cookie Store with SSR Package

Server-side client factory function uses Next.js cookies API with getAll/setAll handlers for session management in Server Components and Route Handlers.

The Supabase server client factory demonstrates the project's pattern for server-side database access. The createClient async function uses Next.js 15's await cookies() from next/headers to access the async cookie store, following the App Router's asynchronous API pattern. It creates a Supabase client using createServerClient from @supabase/ssr package, configured with environment variables NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY using non-null assertions. The cookies configuration provides two methods: getAll() returns all cookies via cookieStore.getAll() for reading session data, and setAll(cookiesToSet) iterates through cookies calling cookieStore.set(name, value, options). The setAll method wraps calls in try-catch, suppressing errors when called from Server Components where cookie mutation fails, deferring to middleware for session refresh. This pattern enables the same createClient function to work in both Route Handlers (where cookies can be set) and Server Components (where they cannot). For P1-04 implementation, this means API routes can use await createClient() to access Supabase for Row Level Security queries, authentication context, and session validation. The pattern shows the project uses Supabase Auth for user identification and RLS for multi-tenant data isolation, which P1-04's API routes must respect by passing authenticated user context to service functions that filter by orgId and check ownership.

# Objectives List and Create API Routes Implemented with Authentication and Validation

GET /api/objectives supports filtering, pagination, and period discovery while POST /api/objectives creates objectives with Zod validation and auth checks.

The first P1-04 API route file implements GET and POST handlers for /api/objectives following Next.js App Router patterns and project conventions. Both handlers begin with authentication using await createClient() to get Supabase client, then supabase.auth.getUser() to verify user session, returning NextResponse.json with 401 status and UNAUTHORIZED code if authentication fails. The GET handler parses query parameters from searchParams extracting 6 filter fields (status, period, teamId, ownerId, parentId, search) and 2 pagination fields (page, limit with defaults '1' and '20'). It validates inputs using objectiveFiltersSchema.parse() and paginationSchema.parse() which coerce string parameters to appropriate types and validate constraints. The handler requires orgId as query parameter with a TODO noting it should come from user profile for proper multi-tenant isolation. It calls getObjectives(orgId, filters, pagination) to fetch paginated data and getDistinctPeriods(orgId) to provide available periods for filter UI, returning combined response with data, meta (page/limit/total/totalPages/hasMore), and filters.periods. The POST handler parses JSON body with await request.json(), validates with createObjectiveSchema.parse() checking title length, date ranges, period format, and required fields, then calls createObjective(validatedData) returning the created objective with 201 status. Both handlers use consistent error handling: ZodError instanceof checks return 400 status with VALIDATION_ERROR code and error.errors details array for client-side field error mapping, while catch-all exceptions log to console and return 500 INTERNAL_ERROR. Response codes (UNAUTHORIZED, MISSING_ORG_ID, VALIDATION_ERROR, INTERNAL_ERROR) provide structured error identification. This establishes the API pattern for subsequent P1-04 routes and future OKR endpoints.

# Progress Ring Component with SVG Circle, Size Variants, and Risk Indication

Client component renders circular progress indicator using SVG stroke-dashoffset animation with three sizes and color-coded risk states.

The ProgressRing component implements a circular progress indicator using SVG technique with stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset. Marked as Client Component ('use client') for DOM interactivity and animations, it accepts progress number, optional size ('sm'|'md'|'lg'), showLabel boolean (default true), className for custom styling, and isAtRisk flag. The sizeConfig object defines three variants: small (40x40px, 4px stroke, text-xs), medium (64x64px, 6px stroke, text-sm), and large (96x96px, 8px stroke, text-lg). The component calculates radius as (width - strokeWidth) / 2, then circumference as radius * 2 * π. Progress is clamped to 0-100 range preventing overflow, then strokeDashoffset is calculated as circumference - (clampedProgress / 100) * circumference, creating the visual arc. The SVG contains two circles: a background circle with stroke-muted class for the track, and a progress circle with strokeDasharray={circumference} and animated strokeDashoffset. The SVG is rotated -90 degrees to position the start at top. Color coding uses getProgressColor function: isAtRisk overrides with stroke-destructive (red), otherwise 100%+ and 70-99% use stroke-green-500, 40-69% use stroke-yellow-500, and 0-39% use stroke-red-500 matching the color thresholds in okr-calculations.ts getProgressColor. The progress circle includes transition-all duration-500 ease-out for smooth animation when progress changes. When showLabel is true, an absolutely positioned span displays the rounded percentage with font-semibold weight, size-appropriate fontSize, and color matching risk state (text-destructive if at-risk, text-foreground otherwise). This reusable component will be used in objective-card.tsx to display objective completion percentage and in future key-result displays.

# Objective Card Component with Status Badges, Progress Ring, and Loading Skeleton

Client component displays objective with French-localized status, date formatting, metadata icons, and skeleton loader for async data.

The ObjectiveCard component renders individual objectives in a visually rich card layout with French localization. Marked as Client Component for interactivity, it accepts objective data, optional progress summary, showActions flag (default true), and className. The StatusBadge helper maps status values to French labels with theme-aware colors: draft uses muted tones, active uses green (bg-green-100/text-green-800 in light mode, bg-green-900/30/text-green-400 in dark), completed uses blue, and archived uses gray. The card structure uses shadcn/ui Card components with condensed spacing (pb-3/pt-3). CardHeader contains a flex layout with left content area and right ProgressRing. The left area displays status badge and period in a flex-wrap row, then CardTitle with clickable Link to /objectives/[id] using hover:underline, and optional CardDescription both with line-clamp-2 for two-line truncation. The ProgressRing displays progressValue (defaulting to 0) with isAtRisk flag determined by presence of at-risk key results. CardContent shows three metadata pieces using lucide-react icons: Calendar icon with French-formatted date range (formatDate uses toLocaleDateString 'fr-FR' locale with day numeric and month short), Target icon with completedKeyResultsCount/keyResultsCount ratio (e.g., "3/5 KRs"), and Users icon when teamId exists. CardFooter renders conditionally based on showActions, containing a ghost variant small Button with asChild Link to detail page showing "Voir détails" with ChevronRight icon. The hover:shadow-md and transition-shadow on Card root provide subtle hover feedback. ObjectiveCardSkeleton mirrors the layout using animated pulse divs: rounded-full for status badge, rectangular shapes for title/description matching widths (3/4 and 1/2), circular shape for progress ring, and smaller rectangles for metadata. This skeleton enables optimistic UI during data loading. The card will be used in objective-list.tsx to display grid/list of objectives and in dashboard widgets.

content:
# Objective Filters Component with URL-Based State and Select Dropdowns

Client component manages search input and status/period/team filters synced to URL query parameters with automatic pagination reset.

The ObjectiveFilters component implements URL-based filter state management using Next.js App Router hooks. Marked as Client Component for router interactions, it accepts optional periods and teams arrays plus className. The component uses useRouter for navigation, usePathname for current path, and useSearchParams for reading query parameters. The createQueryString callback is memoized with useCallback, taking param name and value, creating URLSearchParams from current params, setting the param if value exists and isn't "all" (otherwise deleting it), and crucially deleting the "page" param when any filter changes to reset pagination to page 1 when filters are modified. handleFilterChange constructs query string and calls router.push to update URL triggering re-render. The search input uses a controlled pattern with value from searchParams.get('search') and onChange handler that updates URL on every keystroke. The layout uses space-y-4 vertical spacing with search bar on top (Search icon absolutely positioned left-3 with Input having pl-9 padding), and filter row below using flex-wrap for responsive layout. The Filter icon precedes three Select dropdowns. Status Select always renders with 5 hardcoded options including "Tous les statuts" all value. Period Select conditionally renders when periods.length > 0, populating from props array with "Toutes les périodes" all option. Team Select conditionally renders when teams.length > 0, mapping team objects to SelectItems with id as value and name as label, plus "Toutes les équipes" option. hasActiveFilters checks presence of any filter params, conditionally rendering ghost Button with X icon that calls clearFilters() which navigates to pathname without query string. Note: The component imports Select/SelectContent/SelectItem/SelectTrigger/SelectValue from @/components/ui/select which was not found in the earlier glob search of ui components, indicating this component needs to be added via `npx shadcn@latest add select` before objective-filters.tsx will work. Current values extracted with searchParams.get() defaulting to 'all' for selects and empty string for search, binding Select value props for controlled state. This enables declarative filtering where URL is source of truth, supporting bookmarking, sharing, and browser back/forward navigation.

Faits: ["ObjectiveFilters uses Next.js App Router hooks (useRouter, useSearchParams, usePathname) for URL-based filter state management","Component imports Select from @/components/ui/select which was not in original glob results indicating it needs to be added via shadcn CLI","createQueryString callback manages URLSearchParams setting/deleting params based on value, with automatic page param deletion when filters change for pagination reset","Four filter types supported: search (text input), status (5 options), period (dynamic from props), teamId (dynamic from props)","Status options defined as constant array with French labels: Tous les statuts, Brouillon, Actif, Terminé, Archivé mapped to all/draft/active/completed/archived values","hasActiveFilters boolean checks if any of status/period/teamId/search params exist, conditionally rendering clear filters button","Search input uses controlled component pattern with value from searchParams and onChange calling handleSearchChange to update URL","Period and team filters conditionally rendered only when arrays have length > 0 with \"Toutes\" option for all values"]

# Objective Form with React Hook Form, Zod Validation, and Calendar Date Pickers

Comprehensive form component supporting create/edit modes with 10 fields including French-localized date pickers, conditional rendering, and async submission.

The ObjectiveForm component provides a comprehensive create/edit interface using React Hook Form and Zod validation. Marked as Client Component for form interactivity, it accepts optional objective for editing, required orgId, optional arrays for teams/users/parentObjectives, async onSubmit callback, and isSubmitting flag. The isEditing flag (!!objective) determines resolver schema and button text. useForm initializes with zodResolver using conditional schema selection, defaultValues populating from objective or defaults (title='', period='Q1 2026', status='draft', startDate=now, endDate=+3 months). The form layout uses space-y-6 vertical spacing with 10 FormField components. Title field uses Input with French placeholder and FormDescription helper text. Description uses Textarea with min-h-[100px] and nullish coalescing (value={field.value ?? ''}) handling optional field. Period and Status fields use responsive grid (sm:grid-cols-2) with Select dropdowns: period offers 7 hardcoded 2026 options (Q1-Q4, H1-H2, year), status offers 4 options (Brouillon/Actif/Terminé/Archivé). Date fields use Popover + Calendar pattern: PopoverTrigger wraps outline Button displaying formatted date via date-fns format(field.value, 'PPP', {locale: fr}) showing French format like "22 janvier 2026", CalendarIcon positioned ml-auto, PopoverContent contains Calendar with mode="single" and initialFocus. Owner field maps users array to SelectItems. Team and parentObjective fields conditionally render when arrays populated, both using FormDescription for guidance. The Calendar and Popover components were not found in earlier globs requiring installation via `npx shadcn@latest add calendar popover`. Action buttons use flex justify-end gap-3 pt-4 layout: Cancel button (variant outline) calls router.back() disabled during submission, Submit button shows Loader2 spinner when isSubmitting with conditional text. The handleSubmit wrapper catches errors logging to console. This form enables full CRUD objective management with validation, accessibility, and French localization.

# Objectives List Page with Server-Side Filtering, Suspense Streaming, and Pagination

Server Component page fetches objectives with filters from URL params, renders ObjectiveFilters and ObjectiveList with Suspense boundary for progressive loading.

The objectives list page implements server-side rendering with streaming using React Suspense. As an async Server Component, ObjectivesPage receives searchParams as Promise following Next.js 15 async params API, awaiting it in the component body. The layout uses space-y-6 vertical spacing with header section containing responsive flex (column on mobile, row on desktop) displaying h1 "Objectifs", muted description "Gérez vos objectifs et suivez leur progression", and Button with asChild prop wrapping Link to /objectives/new showing "Nouvel objectif" with Plus icon. The content section wraps ObjectivesContent in Suspense with ObjectivesLoading fallback rendering 6 ObjectiveCardSkeleton components in matching grid layout enabling progressive loading. ObjectivesContent performs authentication via await createClient() and supabase.auth.getUser(), returning unauthenticated message if no user. It constructs filters object from searchParams (status, period, teamId, search) and pagination object parsing page string to integer (default 1) with limit 12. A TODO comment notes orgId should come from user profile but currently uses process.env.DEFAULT_ORG_ID || 'demo-org-id' for development. Promise.all parallelizes fetching getObjectives(orgId, filters, pagination) and getDistinctPeriods(orgId) for filter options. The component renders ObjectiveFilters passing periods array, ObjectiveList passing objectives data with custom emptyMessage, and pagination info section conditionally shown when meta.total > 0 displaying "Affichage de X sur Y objectifs" and page numbers when totalPages > 1. The searchParams integration enables URL-based filter state: changing filters updates URL via router.push in ObjectiveFilters, triggering server-side re-fetch with new params. This provides shareable/bookmarkable filtered views with browser back/forward support. The Suspense boundary allows immediate header/filters render while objectives stream in, improving perceived performance. This completes the list view portion of P1-04's CRUD interface.

# Objective Detail Page with Progress Dashboard, Key Results List, and Hierarchy Display

Server Component page fetches objective with relations showing progress metrics, key results with formatted values, and parent/child objective cards.

The objective detail page provides comprehensive view of a single objective with related data. As async Server Component, it receives params as Promise extracting id, performs authentication via supabase.auth.getUser() calling notFound() if missing. Promise.all parallelizes three data fetches: getObjectiveWithRelations(id) loading objective with owner, team, keyResults (with progress), parent, and children relations; getObjectiveProgress(id) aggregating progress metrics; getChildObjectives(id) for hierarchy display. If objective not found, notFound() is called triggering 404 page. The page calculates statusInfo from statusConfig mapping status to Badge variant and French label, and isAtRisk boolean from atRiskKeyResultsCount. The formatDate helper uses fr-FR locale with full month name format. The layout uses space-y-6 with back button linking to /objectives. The header section uses responsive flex (column on mobile, lg:flex-row on desktop) with left content area showing Badge with status variant, period text, h1 title (text-2xl lg:text-3xl), and optional description (max-w-2xl), paired with right area containing large ProgressRing and Edit button linking to /objectives/[id]/edit. Meta info displays date range, owner name, and team name with Calendar and Users icons. Separator divides header from content. Progress summary renders when progress exists as 4-column responsive grid showing: overall progress percentage, KRs ratio (X/Y format), completed count in green text, at-risk count in red text. Key Results Card has header with title/description and disabled "Ajouter un KR" button (P1-05 functionality). Empty state shows Target icon with message. When KRs exist, space-y-4 list displays each KR in border rounded-lg container with title, optional description, formatted metric values using formatMetricValue (handles percentage/currency/boolean/number with units), weight label, and small ProgressRing showing kr.progress. Child objectives conditionally render in 2-column grid using ObjectiveCard with showActions=false hiding detail link. Parent objective renders single ObjectiveCard when objective.parent exists. This completes the detail view enabling users to see complete objective state, track progress, review KRs, and navigate hierarchy.

Server Component page loads existing objective, filters parent options excluding self, renders ObjectiveForm with update handler redirecting to detail on success.

The edit objective page implements the update interface using Server Component with Server Action pattern. EditObjectivePage receives params.id as Promise, performs authentication check redirecting to /login if user missing, fetches objective via getObjectiveById(id) calling notFound() if not found. Unlike the new page, orgId is extracted from objective.orgId rather than environment variable, showing the objective's actual organization. # Key Result Detail API Route with GET, PUT, DELETE and Check-in Dependency Validation

API endpoints implement detail retrieval with progress summary, update with validation, and delete with check-in dependency check preventing data loss.

The key result detail API route implements GET, PUT, and DELETE operations following the pattern established in objectives routes. All handlers begin with Supabase authentication using await createClient() and supabase.auth.getUser(), returning 401 if authentication fails. The GET handler extracts id from await params, calls getKeyResultWithRelations(id) to fetch the key result with objective, owner, initiatives array, and check-ins sorted descending, returns 404 if not found, then calls getKeyResultProgress(id) to calculate detailed progress metrics including trend, last check-in, days remaining, and at-risk status, spreading both into response with progressSummary field. The PUT handler validates existence via keyResultExists(id) returning 404 if missing, parses JSON body with await request.json(), validates with updateKeyResultSchema.parse() supporting partial updates of fields like title, description, metricType, values, unit, and weight, then calls updateKeyResult(id, validatedData) returning updated resource. The DELETE handler enforces referential integrity by checking existence with keyResultExists and validating no check-ins exist via hasCheckIns(id), returning 400 HAS_DEPENDENCIES with French error message "Impossible de supprimer un Key Result avec des check-ins" preventing deletion of KRs with historical data, only calling deleteKeyResult(id) after validation passes, returning success object. Error handling uses instanceof ZodError for validation errors returning details as error.issues array, and catch-all console.error logging with 500 status. This completes the backend API layer for key results CRUD operations.

Faits: ["GET /api/key-results/[id] fetches key result via getKeyResultWithRelations including objective, owner, initiatives, and check-ins, plus getKeyResultProgress for progressSummary","PUT /api/key-results/[id] validates existence with keyResultExists, parses body with updateKeyResultSchema, and calls updateKeyResult for partial updates","DELETE /api/key-results/[id] checks existence and validates no check-ins via hasCheckIns returning 400 HAS_DEPENDENCIES if check-ins exist","All handlers perform authentication check with supabase.auth.getUser returning 401 UNAUTHORIZED if missing","RouteParams interface types params as Promise with id string following Next.js 15 async params pattern","Error handling returns 404 NOT_FOUND for missing resources, 400 VALIDATION_ERROR for Zod failures with error.issues details, and 500 INTERNAL_ERROR for exceptions"]

# Progress Bar Components with Horizontal Bar Visualization and Metric-Aware Formatting

Client components provide ProgressBar and MetricProgressBar variants with size options, color-coded states, and French-localized metric formatting for currencies and numbers.

Two progress bar components implement horizontal bar visualizations for key results. The base ProgressBar component provides general-purpose progress display accepting value and max (default 100), calculating percentage clamped 0-100, with three size variants defined in sizeClasses (sm: 1.5px, md: 2.5px, lg: 4px height). Optional showLabel displays "Progression" text and showValue shows formatted value using custom formatValue callback or default rounded percentage. The getProgressColor helper returns Tailwind background classes based on thresholds: at-risk flag overrides with bg-red-500, 100%+ uses bg-green-500, 70-99% uses bg-emerald-500, 40-69% uses bg-yellow-500, 0-39% uses bg-orange-500. The MetricProgressBar variant specializes for key result metrics accepting currentValue, startValue, targetValue, unit, and metricType. It calculates progress as ((currentValue - startValue) / (targetValue - startValue)) * 100 handling division by zero with range check, clamping result 0-100. The internal formatMetricValue function provides French-localized formatting: percentage rounds to integer with % suffix, currency uses Intl.NumberFormat with fr-FR locale and EUR currency (no decimals), boolean returns "Oui" for values >= 1 else "Non", number uses toLocaleString('fr-FR') with optional unit suffix. When showDetails=true, MetricProgressBar displays three-column layout: left shows formatted current value in muted color, center shows progress percentage in foreground color (red if at-risk), right shows formatted target value. Both components render bg-muted rounded-full track with inner progress bar div using inline style width percentage, transition-all duration-500 for smooth animations, and ARIA progressbar role with valuenow/valuemin/valuemax attributes for accessibility. These provide horizontal bar alternatives to the circular ProgressRing from objectives, better suited for inline key result displays.

# Ralph Loop Configuration and Development Workflow

Project uses ralph-loop for iterative development with auto-commit, auto-test, and checkpoint promises

The project employs a structured development workflow called "ralph-loop" for iterative task execution. This workflow automation includes automatic commits after successful task completion, automatic test execution to maintain quality gates, and periodic checkpoints every 5 iterations to save progress.

The ralph-loop system uses promise-based completion markers that signal task states: TASK COMPLETE indicates successful task finish, PHASE COMPLETE marks completion of a development phase, TESTS PASS confirms all tests are passing, and BLOCKED - NEED INPUT signals that user intervention is required.

Development follows strict TypeScript conventions with explicit typing requirements for public APIs and preference for interfaces over type aliases for object shapes. The Next.js architecture defaults to Server Components for optimal performance, requiring explicit 'use client' directives only when client-side interactivity is needed, and uses Server Actions for all data mutations to maintain server-side security boundaries.

File naming follows kebab-case for component files (like objective-card.tsx) while the exported component names use PascalCase (ObjectiveCard), maintaining consistency with React ecosystem conventions.

# Agent and Automation Configuration Framework

Mandatory auto-activation rules for Skills, MCP servers, and specialized agents with task execution protocol

The AGENTS.md file establishes a comprehensive automation framework enforcing mandatory use of all available capabilities. The system operates on a strict auto-activation matrix that triggers specific combinations of Skills, MCP servers, and Agents based on detected situations—for example, UI component creation automatically invokes frontend-design skill plus context7 MCP for React patterns.

The configuration includes an autonomous task tracking protocol that reads the .taskmaster/TASKS/tasks-ralph.md file to identify the current task, verify dependencies, generate complete ralph-loop commands, and update task status. The protocol prioritizes tasks by status (in_progress first, then pending by priority level) and validates all dependencies before execution.

Three MCP servers provide core capabilities: context7 for official framework documentation lookup, sequential-thinking for multi-step reasoning on complex problems, and morphllm-fast-apply for bulk code transformations. These integrate with 15 specialized agents that handle specific domains—system-architect for scalability decisions, security-engineer for vulnerability analysis, quality-engineer for testing strategies, etc.

The framework supports multi-IDE development with shared skills between Claude Code (CLI-based) and Antigravity (visual IDE), both accessing the same .agent/skills/ directory containing 233+ skills from the Antigravity Awesome Skills library. Session management requires strict adherence to lifecycle commands: sc:load at session start to restore context, periodic checkpoints every 30 minutes, and sc:save at session end to persist state.

User interaction is streamlined through shortcut commands like "status" to view current task, "go/lance" to execute the generated ralph-loop command, and "next/suivante" to advance to the next pending task. The system enforces prohibitions including never coding UI without frontend-design, never implementing features without sc:implement, and never debugging without sc:troubleshoot plus sequential-thinking.

P1-01 through P1-06 completed with full CRUD for Objectives, Key Results, and Initiatives; P1-07 Check-ins next

The tasks-ralph.md file provides the complete task backlog for the transfo-ia-okr project with detailed Ralph Loop configuration for iterative development. The file tracks 11 total tasks across Phase 0 (Initialization) and Phase 1 (Core Features).

Phase 0 is fully completed, establishing the technical architecture with Next.js 16, Supabase, Prisma 7, and comprehensive tooling including ESLint 9, Prettier, Vitest 4, and GitHub Actions CI. The environment setup delivered 8 Prisma models for the OKR domain, shadcn/ui components, and complete authentication infrastructure.

Phase 1 shows significant progress with 6 of 9 tasks completed (67%). The completed work establishes the full CRUD foundation:
- P1-01: Supabase authentication with email/password, protected routes, middleware, and 13 validation tests
- P1-02: Dashboard layout with responsive sidebar navigation, theme toggle, user menu, breadcrumbs, and 15 component tests
- P1-03: Service layer with 8 CRUD services covering all entities, 20+ Zod validation schemas, OKR calculation utilities, and 89 new tests
- P1-04: Objectives CRUD with API routes, filtering, pagination, hierarchy (parent/children), and complete UI components
- P1-05: Key Results CRUD supporting 4 metric types (percentage, number, currency, boolean) with progress visualization
- P1-06: Initiatives CRUD with status management (todo/in_progress/done), priority levels, grouped lists by status

The next task in queue is P1-07 Check-ins & Progression, which will implement the temporal tracking system for Key Results. This task requires building API routes for check-ins, a form interface capturing value updates with notes and confidence levels, historical timeline display, automatic currentValue updates on Key Results, and progress evolution charts. The task has 6 success criteria all currently unvalidated and is configured for 12 Ralph Loop iterations with checkpoints at iterations 4, 8, and 11.

Following P1-07, two tasks remain: P1-08 for team management with member roles and team-OKR assignments, and P1-09 for the main dashboard with overview widgets, Tremor charts, and at-risk KR identification. P1-09 has dependencies on P1-04, P1-05, and P1-07, requiring the check-in system to be functional before dashboard metrics can be displayed.

# Check-In Service Layer Already Implemented with 17 Functions

Complete CRUD service for check-ins includes automatic KeyResult currentValue updates and statistical operations

The check-in.service.ts file reveals that the check-in service layer was already implemented during Phase 1 Task P1-03 (Service Layer & Types), providing a comprehensive foundation for P1-07 implementation. The service contains 17 well-organized functions grouped into four categories.

READ operations provide flexible data retrieval with seven functions: single check-in by ID (with or without user details), all check-ins for a KeyResult (with optional user includes and limits), check-ins by user, recent organization-wide check-ins with nested objective/KR context, date range queries, and latest check-in retrieval.

WRITE operations implement critical data integrity patterns. The createCheckIn function uses a Prisma transaction to atomically create the check-in record and update the associated KeyResult's currentValue field, ensuring consistency. The deleteCheckIn function is particularly sophisticated—when removing a check-in, it automatically finds the next most recent check-in and updates the KeyResult currentValue accordingly, or reverts to startValue if no check-ins remain.

STATISTICS operations enable progress analysis through getCheckInStats (providing count, average confidence level, and last update timestamp) and getCheckInFrequency (calculating average check-ins per day over a configurable period, defaulting to 30 days).

UTILITY operations provide helper functions for existence checks and counting, supporting validation and business logic requirements. The service integrates with custom types (CheckIn, CheckInWithUser) and validation schemas (CreateCheckInInput) established in the P1-03 type system, demonstrating the layered architecture where services depend on the foundational types and validations.

Faits: ["Check-In Service provides 17 functions across READ, WRITE, STATISTICS, and UTILITY operations","createCheckIn function uses Prisma transaction to atomically create check-in and update KeyResult currentValue","deleteCheckIn automatically recalculates KeyResult currentValue from latest remaining check-in or reverts to startValue","READ operations include getCheckInById, getCheckInWithUser, getCheckInsByKeyResult, getCheckInsByUser, getRecentCheckIns, getCheckInsInDateRange, getLatestCheckIn","Statistical functions include getCheckInStats (count, average confidence, last check-in date) and getCheckInFrequency (check-ins per day)","getRecentCheckIns supports organization-level filtering with nested includes for user and KeyResult/Objective titles","Service supports optional limit parameters on query functions for pagination control","CheckIn model includes keyResultId, userId, value, note, confidence (default 5), and createdAt timestamp","Service ensures data integrity by maintaining KeyResult currentValue consistency through transactional updates"]
