# RealtimeWrapper Client Component Created for Server Component Integration

Wrapper component enables RealtimeProvider usage from Server Component layouts by accepting server-side props and rendering client-side context

A RealtimeWrapper component was created addressing a key architectural challenge in Next.js App Router: integrating Client Components (which use React hooks and context) with Server Components (which fetch data and run on the server). The dashboard layout is a Server Component that extracts user information from Supabase authentication, but RealtimeProvider requires 'use client' marking because it uses useState, useEffect, and Context APIs. The wrapper pattern solves this by creating a minimal Client Component that accepts server-side data as props (userId, userEmail, userName, organizationId) and forwards them to RealtimeProvider with showToasts explicitly set to true. This enables the Server Component layout to remain async and server-rendered while delegating client-side real-time functionality to the wrapper. The component is placed in src/components/providers/ alongside the existing ThemeProvider, establishing a consistent pattern for context providers in the application. This wrapper will be imported and used in the dashboard layout to wrap children, creating the RealtimeProvider context boundary that the PresenceIndicator and future real-time components depend on via useRealtime or useRealtimeOptional hooks.

content:
# Realtime Refresh Hook Created for Automatic Server Component Revalidation

useRealtimeRefresh hook triggers Next.js router.refresh() on OKR changes with debouncing and four specialized variants for different page types

A sophisticated realtime refresh hook was created enabling automatic Server Component revalidation when OKR data changes, completing the real-time update infrastructure for P2-02. The hook addresses a key architectural challenge in Next.js App Router: Server Components fetch data during server-side rendering and cache results, requiring explicit revalidation to display updates. The useRealtimeRefresh hook bridges realtime subscriptions with Next.js's router.refresh() API which triggers Server Component re-execution and data refetching. The implementation uses useRealtimeSubscription hook monitoring specified tables and organizationId, with handleChange callback triggering triggerRefresh on every database change event. The triggerRefresh function implements debouncing to prevent excessive refresh calls: it checks pendingRefreshRef flag returning early if a refresh is already scheduled, clears any existing timeout, sets pending flag true, and schedules router.refresh() and optional onRefresh callback after debounceMs delay (default 500ms), resetting the pending flag afterward. This debouncing is crucial because realtime subscriptions can fire multiple events rapidly (e.g., updating an objective triggers both Objective UPDATE and potentially KeyResult UPDATE events), and each router.refresh() call is expensive as it refetches all Server Component data. The hook provides four specialized variants targeting different page contexts: useObjectivesRefresh monitors Objective and KeyResult tables for objectives list and detail pages; useTeamsRefresh monitors Team table for teams management pages; useCheckInsRefresh monitors CheckIn and KeyResult tables for progress tracking pages; useDashboardRefresh monitors all five OKR tables with extended 1000ms debounce appropriate for the broad dashboard view displaying mixed data. The cleanup effect ensures timeout clearing on unmount preventing memory leaks. This hook enables components to declare their refresh behavior declaratively, for example an objectives list page can call useObjectivesRefresh() causing the list to automatically refresh when other users create, update, or delete objectives, fulfilling P2-02 success criteria for "Mise à jour live des listes (objectives, key-results)".

Faits: ["useRealtimeRefresh hook created at src/hooks/use-realtime-refresh.ts with 116 lines implementing automatic page refresh on realtime changes","Hook uses Next.js useRouter().refresh() to revalidate Server Components fetching fresh data from Supabase","Debounce mechanism with configurable delay (default 500ms) prevents excessive refresh calls from rapid change events","pendingRefresh flag prevents duplicate refresh scheduling when debounce timer is active","Four specialized hook variants exported: useObjectivesRefresh (Objective+KeyResult tables), useTeamsRefresh (Team table), useCheckInsRefresh (CheckIn+KeyResult), useDashboardRefresh (all tables, 1000ms debounce)","Hook returns connectionState, isConnected, and triggerRefresh function enabling manual refresh invocation","Cleanup effect clears pending timeouts on unmount preventing memory leaks and stale refresh calls"]
summary: Realtime Refresh Hook Created for Automatic Server Component Revalidation

# P2-03 Export Architecture Design with jsPDF and Native CSV Generation

Sequential thinking analysis establishes API design with streaming support and lightweight client-side PDF generation approach

The primary session initiated a sequential thinking analysis via MCP to design the architecture for task P2-03 Export Functionality. The first thought establishes the foundation by analyzing the existing context (Next.js 16, Prisma 7, Supabase with completed Phase 1 services) and proposing a comprehensive export architecture. A critical architectural decision was made to use jsPDF with jspdf-autotable for PDF generation rather than @react-pdf/renderer, prioritizing lightweight implementation and client-side compatibility. CSV generation will leverage native JavaScript capabilities without external dependencies. The export system will support four distinct CSV formats covering objectives, key results, check-ins, and combined reports, plus three PDF report types for individual objectives, team-level summaries, and organization-wide reports. The API design employs a unified endpoint (/api/export) with query parameters for format type and entity selection, incorporating streaming capabilities to handle large data exports efficiently. The UI layer is structured into three component levels: ExportButton for triggering actions, ExportDialog for user format and scope selection, and ExportOptions for granular configuration. This represents thought 1 of 5 in the sequential analysis, with more detailed planning to follow.

The type system is comprehensively structured with enums defining all status values and classifications across the OKR hierarchy. Base entity interfaces (Organization, Team, User, Objective, KeyResult, Initiative, CheckIn, Comment) map directly to Prisma schema models with typed fields including ID strings, dates, and nullable fields. Extended relation types layer on top, providing different views of data: ObjectiveWithKeyResults for basic nesting, ObjectiveWithRelations for complete object graphs including owner, team, parent/children hierarchy, and key results with their progress. Period helper functions support parsing and generating date ranges for quarters (Q1-Q4), half-years (H1-H2), and full years, enabling period-based filtering and reporting in exports. This comprehensive type system will guide the export data structure design and ensure type safety across CSV and PDF generation.

# Context7 Provides jsPDF Implementation Patterns for Node.js and AutoTable

Documentation shows jsPDF automatically loads Node.js version, autoTable plugin for tables, and text formatting methods for PDF generation

The primary session queried Context7 documentation for jsPDF implementation patterns focusing on server-side Node.js usage and table generation. The documentation confirms jsPDF's seamless Node.js support, automatically detecting the environment and loading appropriate APIs with file system operations for saving PDFs. The integration is straightforward with require or import statements, and doc.save() writes directly to the filesystem. The jspdf-autotable plugin emerges as the primary mechanism for table generation, accepting structured data as head (header rows) and body (data rows) arrays with configuration options like startY for vertical positioning. Text formatting capabilities include setFontSize for size control, setFont for font family selection (five built-in fonts available), and setFontType for style variants (normal, bold, italic, bolditalic). The text method positions content via x,y coordinates. This documentation validates the architectural decision from sequential thinking to use jsPDF with jspdf-autotable, confirming both libraries work in Next.js API routes (Node.js environment) and provide the necessary features for generating professional PDF reports with formatted text and tables. The implementation will use ES modules (import) syntax matching the project's TypeScript configuration.

# P2-03 Implementation Plan with 5-Phase Phased Approach

Phase B builds the service layer orchestration in export.service.ts, defining six exported functions with clear signatures: three CSV exporters (objectives, key results, check-ins) accepting orgId and filters, and three PDF report generators (objective, team, organization) returning formatted documents. Phase C implements the API layer with a single /api/export route using query parameters for flexible export requests - format parameter selects CSV or PDF, type parameter specifies data scope (objectives/key-results/check-ins/team/organization), id parameter targets specific entities, and teamId enables filtering. # CSV Generator Utility Implemented with Type-Safe Column Definitions

Native JavaScript CSV generation with UTF-8 BOM encoding, proper escaping, configurable formatting, and predefined columns for all OKR entity types

The primary session implemented the CSV generator utility as Phase A of the P2-03 implementation plan. The file provides a robust native JavaScript CSV generation system without external dependencies. The core generateCSV function accepts generic typed data arrays and CSVColumn definitions, supporting both direct property access and computed accessor functions for flexible data transformation. The implementation handles CSV special characters properly according to RFC 4180 standards - values containing commas, quotes, or line breaks are wrapped in double quotes with internal quotes escaped by doubling. UTF-8 BOM encoding is enabled by default to ensure Excel opens files with correct character encoding without requiring manual import configuration. Date formatting offers three options: ISO 8601 for machine readability, French locale format, and short DD/MM/YYYY format for user-friendly reports. Five comprehensive column definition arrays are pre-configured for each OKR entity type: objectives export includes 11 fields with progress percentage and related entity names, key results export has 13 fields covering all metric types and progress tracking, check-ins export captures 7 fields including confidence levels, teams export shows 6 fields with aggregate counts, and initiatives export provides 9 fields with status and priority. The column definitions leverage TypeScript intersection types to extend base entity types with optional computed fields, maintaining type safety while supporting enriched export data. Helper functions csvToBlob and generateFileName complete the utility API for file download workflows.

# Export Service Implemented with 8 Functions for CSV and PDF Generation

Complete service layer orchestrating data aggregation from Prisma, progress calculations, and export generation for all OKR entity types

The primary session implemented the export service completing Phase B of the P2-03 implementation plan. The service orchestrates complete export workflows by composing existing services and utilities. Five CSV export functions cover all OKR entities: exportObjectivesToCSV queries objectives with team and owner relations, calculates weighted progress by aggregating key result progress values multiplied by weights, and enriches with teamName and ownerName before generating CSV; exportKeyResultsToCSV includes objective titles and calculates individual progress; exportCheckInsToCSV supports date range filtering and includes user names; exportInitiativesToCSV includes key result titles; exportTeamsToCSV uses Prisma _count aggregations for member and objective counts. Three PDF report generators create professional multi-page documents: generateObjectiveReport produces portrait-oriented reports with general information table, description text with word wrapping, progress statistics (3 stat cards showing overall progress, KR count, completed count), key results table with current/target values, and initiatives table with status/priority; generateTeamReport creates team summaries with 4 stat cards, member listing with roles, and objectives table with calculated per-objective weighted progress; generateOrganizationReport generates landscape-oriented executive summaries with 6 stat cards across the top, team summary table showing member counts and average progress per team, and active objectives list limited to 15 entries with truncated titles. All PDF reports leverage the utility functions for consistent formatting: branded headers with centered titles and generation timestamps, automatic footers with page numbers and branding, section headers, stat cards with colored top bars, tables with autoTable styled consistently, French date formatting and status translations. Progress calculations use the existing calculateKeyResultProgress utility ensuring consistency with dashboard displays. The service returns CSV as strings and PDF as Uint8Array (arraybuffer output from jsPDF) ready for API route transmission.

content:
# Export API Route Implemented with Authentication and Format Validation

GET /api/export endpoint handles 8 export types with parameter validation, Supabase auth check, org-scoped filtering, and proper HTTP headers for downloads

The primary session implemented the export API route completing Phase C of the P2-03 implementation plan. The endpoint provides a unified interface for all export functionality via GET /api/export with query parameters. Authentication is enforced at the route level: the handler first checks Supabase authentication with getUser(), returns 401 Unauthorized if no user session exists, then queries the User table to retrieve the user's orgId, returning 400 Bad Request if the user is not associated with an organization. This ensures all exports are automatically scoped to the authenticated user's organization. Parameter validation is comprehensive: format must be 'csv' or 'pdf', type must be one of eight valid values, and id parameter is required for the three report types (objective-report, team-report require id, organization-report uses orgId). The ExportFilters object is constructed from optional query parameters including period, teamId, status for filtering entity lists, and startDate/endDate for check-ins temporal filtering. A switch statement routes requests to the appropriate export service function: five CSV exporters (objectives, key-results, check-ins, initiatives, teams) and three PDF report generators. Each case validates format compatibility (CSV-only types reject PDF requests and vice versa), calls the service function with appropriate parameters, and generates a timestamped filename. The response construction sets proper HTTP headers: Content-Type specifies text/csv with UTF-8 charset or application/pdf, Content-Disposition attachment header triggers browser download with generated filename, and Cache-Control directives prevent caching of dynamic exports. Error handling catches exceptions, logs them to console, returns 404 for "not found" errors, and 500 for general failures. The NextResponse returns the data (string for CSV, Uint8Array for PDF) with configured headers, completing the server-side export workflow.

Faits: ["API route /api/export implements GET handler accepting query parameters: format (csv/pdf), type (8 valid types), id (for reports), period, teamId, status, startDate, endDate","Authentication flow uses Supabase auth.getUser() check, queries User table for orgId, returns 401 if unauthorized or 400 if no organization","Eight export types supported: objectives, key-results, check-ins, initiatives, teams (CSV only), objective-report, team-report, organization-report (PDF only)","Parameter validation ensures format is csv or pdf, type is valid, and id parameter is present for individual report types","Switch statement routes to appropriate export service function with orgId and filters, generates timestamped filename via generateFileName utility","Response headers include Content-Type (text/csv or application/pdf), Content-Disposition with attachment and filename, Cache-Control no-cache directives","Error handling catches errors, returns 404 for not found messages, 500 for general failures, logs errors to console","CSV exports support filtering by period/teamId/status, check-ins support date range filtering via startDate/endDate"]
summary: Export API Route Implemented with Authentication and Format Validation

# ExportButton Component with Adaptive UI and Preset Configurations

Client component handles export downloads with single/dropdown modes, loading states, toast notifications, and 5 predefined option sets for different pages

The primary session implemented the ExportButton component completing Phase D of the P2-03 implementation plan. This client component provides a flexible export trigger with adaptive UI based on the number of options: rendering a simple button when only one export option is provided, or a dropdown menu when multiple options are available. The core handleExport async function orchestrates the download workflow: it constructs a URLSearchParams object from the provided filters (period, teamId, status, startDate, endDate) and entityId, fetches the /api/export endpoint, validates the response, extracts the filename from the Content-Disposition header using regex matching, converts the response to a blob, creates an object URL, programmatically triggers download via a temporary anchor element, and cleans up by revoking the object URL and removing the anchor. Loading state management provides visual feedback with isExporting boolean tracking overall state and exportingType tracking which specific export is running, displaying a Loader2 spinner icon during exports and disabling interactive elements. Toast notifications enhance UX with success messages showing the export label and error messages displaying the error text. The component accepts optional callbacks onExportSuccess and onExportError for parent components to handle export lifecycle events. Five predefined option preset arrays simplify integration: objectivesExportOptions provides objectives CSV, key-results CSV, and organization PDF report; singleObjectiveExportOptions provides a single objective PDF report; teamsExportOptions provides teams CSV; singleTeamExportOptions provides team PDF report; analyticsExportOptions provides all four data types (objectives, key-results, check-ins CSVs plus organization PDF). Icon usage differentiates formats visually: FileSpreadsheet for CSV exports, FileText for PDF reports, Download generic icon for the dropdown trigger. The dropdown menu displays option labels with optional descriptions in smaller muted text. The component properly extends ButtonProps, allowing customization of variant, size, and other button properties while omitting the onClick handler that's internally managed.

# ExportDialog Component with Form Configuration and Dynamic Filters

Modal dialog provides export configuration interface with type selection, format options, period/team filters, and validates ID requirements for report types

The primary session implemented the ExportDialog component continuing Phase D of the P2-03 implementation plan. This modal dialog provides a comprehensive export configuration interface beyond the simpler ExportButton component. The EXPORT_CONFIGS constant defines complete metadata for all eight export types: five CSV-only types (objectives, key-results, check-ins, initiatives, teams) and three PDF-only types (objective-report, team-report, organization-report), with needsId: true flags marking the two report types requiring entity IDs. Form state management uses React hooks to track four selection values: selectedType and selectedFormat for the core export configuration, selectedPeriod and selectedTeam for optional filtering. A useEffect hook ensures format compatibility by automatically resetting selectedFormat when the user changes selectedType to a type that doesn't support the currently selected format. The UI adapts dynamically based on configuration: the format selector only renders when the current type supports multiple formats (none currently do, but the structure supports future expansion), period and team filter selectors render only for CSV exports when availableFilters data is provided. The type selector intelligently filters options, hiding report types that require an entityId when the entityId prop is not provided, preventing user frustration from selecting unavailable options. The handleExport async function mirrors ExportButton's download logic: validates ID requirements against the config, constructs URLSearchParams with type, format, optional entityId, and filter values, fetches /api/export, extracts filename from headers, creates blob download via object URL and temporary anchor, displays success toast, closes the dialog, and invokes the onExportSuccess callback. The component accepts a custom trigger element via the trigger prop, defaulting to an outline variant button with Download icon and "Exporter" label. The dialog uses shadcn/ui components for consistent styling with header, description, form fields with labels, and footer with cancel and export action buttons showing loading state during export.

Phase 0-1 complete (9 tasks), Phase 2 in progress with 4 advanced features pending including AI-powered suggestions.

The transfo-ia-okr project tracks development progress through a structured task backlog in tasks-ralph.md with Ralph Loop automation. Phase 0 established the technical foundation with architecture documentation and Next.js 16 environment setup including Prisma ORM with 8 models, Supabase authentication, ESLint 9 flat config, and Vitest testing framework. Phase 1 delivered 9 core features: Supabase email/password authentication with middleware protection, responsive dashboard layout with sidebar navigation and dark mode, comprehensive service layer for all OKR entities, full CRUD operations for objectives with hierarchical relationships, key results supporting 4 metric types (percentage/number/currency/boolean), initiatives with status tracking, check-ins system with automatic currentValue updates and progress charts, team management with hierarchical structure and member roles, and main dashboard with overview statistics and activity widgets. Phase 2 advances with analytics using Recharts library (5 chart types), real-time updates via Supabase Realtime with presence indicators and toast notifications, and PDF/CSV export functionality using jsPDF and autoTable. # Prisma client singleton pattern examined for Gemini client implementation

The src/lib/db.ts file was examined as the reference implementation for creating a singleton client pattern. Both named and default exports provide import flexibility. This pattern should be adapted for gemini-client.ts with GoogleGenAI replacing PrismaClient, GEMINI_API_KEY environment variable instead of DATABASE_URL, and similar environment-based configuration for model selection and logging.

# OKR suggestion prompts implemented with expert persona and structured templates

198-line prompt engineering module with three system prompts, three prompt builders, and JSON response parser for structured AI outputs.

The OKR suggestion prompts were implemented as src/lib/ai/prompts/okr-suggestions.ts, establishing the domain-specific intelligence layer. The 198-line module defines three tiers of system prompts: the base SYSTEM_PROMPT_OKR_EXPERT establishes an expert persona with 15 years experience in OKR methodology, John Doerr's framework, SMART objectives, strategic alignment, and performance measurement, with explicit instructions for French responses, concise actionable advice, concrete examples, bullet-point structure, and professional accessible tone. SYSTEM_PROMPT_OBJECTIVE_IMPROVEMENT extends the base prompt with specific guidance for improving objective formulation, emphasizing inspirational ambitious language, qualitative focus without metrics, time-boundedness, strategic alignment, and universal comprehensibility, requesting improved formulation, 2-3 alternatives, strengths, and improvement axes. SYSTEM_PROMPT_KEY_RESULTS_GENERATION focuses on suggesting measurable KRs with clear metrics, ambitious but attainable targets (70-80% success rate), time constraints, direct objective linkage, and independence between KRs, requesting 3-5 diversified suggestions with title, metric type, start/target values, and justification. Three prompt builder functions construct user prompts: buildObjectiveImprovementPrompt() and buildKeyResultsSuggestionPrompt() both accept ObjectiveContext with title, optional description, period, team name, and existing KRs (to avoid duplication), while buildKeyResultImprovementPrompt() accepts KeyResultContext with parent objective, title, metrics, and current progress. The KR suggestion prompt includes a JSON response format specification ensuring structured outputs. The parseKeyResultsSuggestion() parser extracts JSON from potentially text-wrapped responses using regex matching, validates array structure, normalizes each KR with type coercion (String/Number), validates metric types against the four allowed values matching MetricType enum from src/types/okr.ts, and defaults to percentage if invalid. This prompt engineering layer transforms the generic Gemini model into a specialized OKR consultant providing contextually relevant, actionable, and correctly structured advice.

# Risk analysis prompts implemented with temporal progress tracking and structured recommendations

192-line module with risk analyst persona, comprehensive context evaluation, four risk levels, and dual parsers for structured and quick recommendations.

The risk analysis prompt system was implemented as src/lib/ai/prompts/risk-analysis.ts, providing intelligent OKR risk assessment capabilities. The 192-line module extends the OKR expert persona with SYSTEM_PROMPT_RISK_ANALYST which defines a structured risk evaluation framework. Five key factors guide the analysis: progression compared to time elapsed (the critical metric for detecting delays), recent trends showing improvement or deterioration, confidence levels from check-ins indicating team sentiment, gap between current and target values showing remaining distance, and complexity/dependencies highlighting external constraints. Four risk levels map to color-coded actions: low/green for on-track objectives, moderate/yellow for slight delays requiring attention, high/orange for significant delays demanding corrective actions, and critical/red for compromised objectives needing escalation. The RiskAnalysisContext interface captures comprehensive context including objective metadata (title, description, period, dates, status), detailed key results array with metrics (progress percentages, values, trends, last check-in dates, confidence scores), aggregated statistics (overallProgress), and temporal tracking (daysElapsed, daysTotal, timeProgress percentage). The buildRiskAnalysisPrompt() function constructs rich prompts calculating progress gaps for both objective and individual key results, formatting trends with Unicode arrows (↑ up, ↓ down, → stable), and specifying a structured JSON response format with risk level, numerical score, summary, factors with impact classification (positive/negative/neutral), recommendation list, and key metrics to watch. An alternative buildQuickRecommendationsPrompt() provides lightweight functionality for rapid 3-recommendation generation when full analysis isn't needed. Two parsers handle responses: parseRiskAnalysis() uses regex to extract JSON from text-wrapped responses, validates structure, normalizes risk level to valid enum values with moderate as fallback, clamps score to 0-100 range, and ensures arrays for factors/recommendations/metrics with empty array fallbacks; parseQuickRecommendations() parses numbered list items from text responses with max 5 returned. This risk analysis system provides actionable intelligence for identifying at-risk objectives, understanding root causes, and generating concrete corrective actions.

# AI suggestions API route implemented with validation, rate limiting, and error handling

236-line POST endpoint supporting three suggestion types with Zod validation, in-memory rate limiter (10 req/min), and structured JSON parsing.

The AI suggestions API route was implemented as src/app/api/ai/suggest/route.ts providing the POST /api/ai/suggest endpoint. The 236-line module handles three suggestion types through a comprehensive validation and execution pipeline. Three Zod schemas validate inputs: ObjectiveContextSchema requires title and period with optional description, teamName, and existingKeyResults array; KeyResultContextSchema requires objectiveTitle, title, metricType, and three numeric values; SuggestionRequestSchema wraps these with a type discriminator enum. In-memory rate limiting prevents abuse using a Map to track IP addresses (from x-forwarded-for header or 'anonymous' fallback) with 10 requests per minute limit and 60-second rolling window. The POST handler executes a six-step flow: first checks Gemini availability returning 503 if unconfigured, validates rate limit returning 429 if exceeded, parses and validates JSON body with Zod returning 400 with flattened errors if invalid, builds appropriate prompt via switch statement selecting system prompt and prompt builder function, calls generateContent() with 1500 max tokens and 0.7 temperature, and optionally parses JSON responses for suggest_key_results requests using parseKeyResultsSuggestion() returning both structured and raw data. Error handling provides specific responses for quota/rate errors (429), API key errors (500), and generic API failures (500) with console logging for debugging. A bonus GET handler returns service availability status and model identifier for health monitoring. This implementation provides a production-ready endpoint with proper validation, rate limiting, error handling, and structured responses following the patterns established in existing API routes like /api/export.

# Risk analysis API route implemented with dual analysis modes and stricter rate limiting

232-line POST endpoint supporting full analysis and quick recommendations with 5 requests/minute limit and graceful parse error handling.

The risk analysis API route was implemented as src/app/api/ai/analyze/route.ts providing POST /api/ai/analyze for OKR risk assessment. The 232-line module supports two distinct analysis modes via type discriminator. The validation layer includes KeyResultAnalysisSchema capturing 9 fields (title, metricType, three values, progress, optional lastCheckInDate, lastConfidence 0-5, trend enum) and RiskAnalysisRequestSchema with objective metadata, optional keyResults/progress/timing arrays, and type enum. Rate limiting is stricter than the suggest endpoint at 5 requests per minute (vs 10) recognizing that risk analysis is computationally heavier and typically less frequent. The POST handler diverges based on analysis type: full_analysis validates keyResults presence returning 400 if missing, constructs RiskAnalysisContext with nullish coalescing defaults (90 days total, 0 for numeric metrics), calls generateContent with 2000 max tokens and temperature 0.5 for more deterministic analytical output, attempts parseRiskAnalysis() and returns structured response with both parsed and raw data, or falls back to a moderate-risk default structure with parseError flag if parsing fails. Quick_recommendations mode skips context construction, builds a lightweight prompt with buildQuickRecommendationsPrompt(), uses 500 tokens and temperature 0.7, parses numbered list responses, and falls back to returning raw response as single-item array if parsing yields empty results. This graceful degradation ensures the API always returns usable data even when JSON extraction fails. Error handling mirrors the suggest endpoint with quota/rate detection returning 429 and generic failures returning 500 with console logging. The GET endpoint adds transparency by exposing the rate limit threshold (5) alongside availability status. This implementation provides production-ready risk analysis with appropriate cost controls, validation, and error recovery.

The AI suggest button component was implemented in src/components/ai/ai-suggest-button.tsx as a flexible client component. The 173-line module exports AiSuggestButton with three semantic variants configured in VARIANT_CONFIG: improve uses Wand2 icon with violet color scheme (hover:bg-violet-50) for refinement suggestions, generate uses Sparkles icon with amber theme for creating new content, and analyze uses Lightbulb icon with blue theme for risk assessment. Each variant defines icon component, French label, loading message, tooltip text, and Tailwind className for hover states. The component accepts comprehensive props including variant enum, boolean flags for loading/disabled/unavailable/showLabel states, optional tooltip override, className for styling, onClick callback, and size enum matching shadcn/ui Button sizes. The rendering logic has three branches: if unavailable is true, the button is wrapped in a Tooltip showing AlertTriangle icon with "Service IA non disponible" message and cursor-not-allowed styling, preventing interaction when the backend is misconfigured; if tooltip prop exists or showLabel is false, the button is wrapped in TooltipProvider with either custom or default variant tooltip; otherwise the bare button is returned. The button content conditionally shows AiLoadingIndicator with variant-specific message during loading, or the variant icon with optional label text otherwise. The disabled state combines disabled, isLoading, and unavailable flags ensuring no interaction during operations or service outages. A bonus AiBadge component provides a small amber rounded badge with Sparkles icon and "IA" text for labeling AI-generated content, useful for transparency and attribution in UI. This button provides a polished, accessible interface for triggering AI operations with clear visual feedback for different action types and system states.

# Inline suggestion component implemented with multi-state rendering and risk level indicator

264-line module exports AiInlineSuggestion with five conditional states and three visual variants plus RiskLevelIndicator badge for risk assessment display.

The inline suggestion component was implemented as src/components/ai/ai-inline-suggestion.tsx for contextual AI feedback display. The 264-line module exports AiInlineSuggestion designed for embedding directly in forms or pages rather than modal dialogs. The component handles five conditional states with early returns: isLoading shows AiPulseIndicator with "Analyse en cours..." using the variant-specific styling; error renders a red-bordered alert with AlertCircle icon, error title and message, and optional dismiss button; empty state (no suggestions or message) returns null for clean unmounting; single message mode displays Lightbulb icon with custom message text in amber theme; suggestions list mode renders the full interactive interface. Three variant styles provide contextual flexibility: card uses gradient bg-gradient-to-br from amber to orange with rounded border and padding for prominent display, banner uses horizontal border-y for full-width inline placement, compact reduces padding and uses simple border for tight spaces. The suggestions list features numbered badges (amber circular backgrounds with 1-based indices), suggestion text, and individual apply buttons. Local state tracks appliedIndex enabling per-suggestion visual feedback with green border and "Appliqué" text after application. The collapsible prop adds ChevronDown/ChevronUp toggle button allowing users to collapse the suggestion list while keeping the header visible. The onDismiss callback adds an X button for complete removal. A bonus RiskLevelIndicator component provides color-coded risk badges with RISK_CONFIG mapping four levels to French labels and Tailwind color classes: low/Faible (green), moderate/Modéré (yellow), high/Élevé (orange), critical/Critique (red). The indicator supports optional score percentage display with 75% opacity, showLabel toggle, and three size variants (sm/md/lg) for flexible integration in dashboards and detail views. These inline components enable contextual AI assistance without disrupting workflow, appearing directly where users need guidance.

# AI suggestion handlers implemented for requesting and applying suggestions

Two handler functions added: handleRequestAiSuggestion builds ObjectiveContext and opens dialog, handleApplySuggestion extracts improved title via regex and updates form.

Two handler functions were added to manage AI suggestion interactions in the objective form. The handleRequestAiSuggestion function captures current form state by calling form.getValues(), resolves the optional teamName by finding the team object matching teamId and accessing its name property (with optional chaining for safety), constructs an ObjectiveContext object with title, description, period, and teamName fields matching the prompt template interface, calls the requestSuggestion method from the useAiSuggestion hook with improve_objective type and the context, and finally sets aiDialogOpen to true to display the modal. This provides all necessary context for the AI to generate SMART objective recommendations. The handleApplySuggestion function processes the AI-generated text by attempting to extract an improved title using a regex pattern that matches common French response formats like "version améliorée:", "suggestion:", or "titre:" followed by the actual title text potentially wrapped in French guillemets (« ») or English quotes. If a match is found, it updates the title form field using form.setValue triggering React Hook Form's validation and state management. The dialog is then closed and the suggestion state cleared to prepare for potential subsequent requests. These handlers complete the interactive flow where users can request suggestions with current form values and selectively apply improvements back to the form fields.

User clarified conversational agent must transform collected transformation context into measurable variables like INIT1 model for tracking mission impact and OKR progression

A critical architectural clarification emerged for P2-05 regarding the output format and purpose of the conversational transformation agent. The user emphasized that the application's core objective is not merely documenting transformation context, but measuring the impact of each action within a mission and tracking the evolution of indicators, curves, progressions, and OKRs over time. The collected transformation data from conversations (whether technical, organizational, or business domains) must be transformed into measurable variables that can be quantitatively tracked, similar to the INIT1.md model which defines variables like adoption_rate, trust_index, proof_density, quality_stability, value_perceived, risk_perceived, effort_to_try, and use_case metrics. This means P2-05 requires not just a chat interface with structured summaries, but also a variable extraction and mapping layer that converts qualitative conversational input into quantitative metrics suitable for dashboard visualization, trend analysis, and OKR progression tracking. The INIT1.md file serves as a reference example showing how transformation concepts can be operationalized as measurable variables - this pattern should be applied to technical transformations (latency metrics, availability percentages, test coverage), organizational transformations (eNPS scores, time-to-market reductions, adoption rates), and business transformations (NPS deltas, revenue growth percentages, conversion rate improvements). The architecture must therefore include variable schema definition for each transformation type, extraction logic that parses conversation outputs into variable assignments, persistence of variable values with timestamps for trend tracking, and integration with the existing OKR system to link transformation variables to key result metrics. This clarification significantly impacts the data model, requiring not just TransformationSession and TransformationField tables, but also TransformationVariable tables with value tracking over time, potentially linked to KeyResult entities for impact measurement.

# P2-06 Document Analysis Agent Task Added to Backlog

New task specification for AI-powered document analysis agent that automatically updates transformation indicators from uploaded progress reports and documents

A new Phase 2 task P2-06 was added to the project backlog, specifying a document analysis agent for continuous transformation tracking. This high-priority feature extends P2-05's conversational transformation setup by enabling ongoing monitoring through document ingestion. The agent analyzes user-uploaded documents (progress reports, meeting minutes, metrics analyses, action notes, key communications) using Google Gemini API to automatically extract transformation indicators. The system architecture implements a three-stage pipeline: document input accepts multiple formats, AI analysis extracts relevant information and maps it to existing session variables while detecting progression/regression signals and identifying quantifiable metrics, and automatic updates propose changes to variables/indicators, progression curves, and OKR check-ins with deviation alerts. The UX emphasizes user control with mandatory validation before applying changes - the system displays proposed updates with justifications, user confirms or adjusts, then changes apply with full history tracking. This prevents blind automated modifications that could corrupt transformation data. The agent provides intelligent context-aware extraction linked to the specific transformation session, detects inconsistencies or contradictions, and generates proactive alerts for risks, drift, or delays. Implementation requires 18 new files including specialized prompts for document analysis and variable extraction, a document analysis service orchestrating the pipeline, four API routes handling the analysis workflow (analyze, list analyses, get analysis, apply analysis), three pages for upload/analysis/history interfaces, six UI components for document handling and result presentation, a custom hook for analysis state management, and comprehensive tests. The feature depends on P2-05's transformation session infrastructure and extends it with continuous data ingestion capabilities, transforming the system from one-time strategic discovery to ongoing transformation monitoring and tracking.

# P2-05 Task Title and Purpose Updated to Emphasize Variable Transformation

Task renamed to "Agent d'Initialisation de Transformation" with explicit Conversation → Variables flow for T0 baseline and target generation

The P2-05 task specification was refined to clarify its role as an initialization agent that runs at the start of a transformation mission. The new title "Agent d'Initialisation de Transformation (Conversation → Variables)" explicitly communicates the core transformation process from qualitative conversational input to quantitative measurable variables. A new primary objective diagram was added showing the complete flow: user provides information through guided conversation based on FORMULAIRES.txt templates, the system extracts and transforms this textual context into structured variables with numerical scores (0-1 range), percentages, and categorical states, establishing both T0 baseline measurements (current state at transformation start) and target variable values (desired future state objectives), which feed into automatic OKR generation. This clarification addresses the user's concern that the application's core purpose is measuring transformation impact and tracking indicator evolution over time, not merely documenting context. The T0 baseline concept is critical as it establishes the measurement foundation from which all future progress will be calculated - without quantified starting values, impact measurement becomes impossible. The target variables represent the transformation goals translated into measurable metrics, enabling the system to track gaps between current and desired states, calculate progression percentages, generate trend curves, and trigger alerts when trajectories diverge from plans. This positions P2-05 as the initialization phase that bootstraps the entire measurement system, while subsequent tasks like P2-06 (document analysis) will handle ongoing variable updates as the transformation progresses.

# P2-05 Task Decomposed into 7 Granular Subtasks for Incremental Implementation

Monolithic transformation agent task split into modular subtasks covering Prisma schema, TypeScript types, AI prompts, services/APIs, chat streaming, UI components, and OKR integration

The P2-05 transformation initialization agent task was refactored from a single complex specification into 7 focused subtasks to improve implementation granularity and reduce risk. The original monolithic task with 25 Ralph Loop iterations, 19 success criteria, and 27 files to create has been decomposed into manageable units that can be developed, tested, and validated independently. The decomposition follows logical architectural layers: P2-05a establishes the Prisma data models (TransformationSession, TransformationField, TransformationVariable, ChatMessage) with proper relations, P2-05b defines comprehensive TypeScript types including transformation types enum, axis definitions, variable structures, chat message types, and API DTOs. P2-05d implements the service layer and REST API endpoints for CRUD operations on transformation sessions with field and variable management. P2-05e builds the chat streaming API using Server-Sent Events with persona orchestration, automatic variable extraction triggers, message persistence, and conversation context tracking. P2-05f develops React UI components for the chat interface including message bubbles with markdown support, auto-resizing input, typing indicators, and type badges with proper ARIA accessibility. P2-05g completes the implementation with transformation list and detail pages, progress indicators, structured summaries with variable tables, and OKR export functionality that generates objectives and key results from collected variables. This decomposition provides better incremental progress visibility, clearer testing boundaries, reduced blast radius for issues, and enables potential parallel development once early dependencies are satisfied. # P2-05 Task Decomposed into 7 Subtasks with Hybrid Architecture Specification

P2-05 split into sequential subtasks (a-g) implementing conversation-to-variables transformation agent with unified chat interface and three specialized personas

The P2-05 conversational transformation agent was decomposed into 7 sequential subtasks to manage implementation complexity. The architecture was finalized as a hybrid approach combining a unified chat interface with AI-powered routing to three specialized personas (Technical, Organizational, Business/Métier) that can handle single-type or hybrid multi-domain transformations. The core workflow transforms conversational input into measurable variables establishing T0 baseline and target values, which then generate linked OKR structures. This initialization phase (P2-05) separates cleanly from the continuous tracking phase (P2-06) that will analyze uploaded documents to evolve variables over time. The reference document FORMULAIRES - Orchestration.txt structures questions across three transformation types with 12-14 axes each covering technical concerns (performance, architecture, APIs), organizational dynamics (culture, change management, human impacts), and business dimensions (customer value, competition, go-to-market). Four Prisma models support the system: TransformationSession tracks overall transformation initiatives with type (TECHNICAL/ORGANIZATIONAL/BUSINESS/HYBRID) and status; TransformationField stores conversational responses by axis with metadata; TransformationVariable maintains T0 baseline, target, and current values for extracted metrics; ChatMessage preserves conversation history. The INIT1.md agent-based model provides concrete variable examples spanning global system metrics, individual agent perceptions, and use-case scores. The 7-subtask decomposition sequences work logically: schema/migration foundation (P2-05a), TypeScript type definitions (P2-05b), AI prompt engineering for three personas (P2-05c), session management services and APIs (P2-05d), streaming chat API endpoint (P2-05e), React chat UI components (P2-05f), and final page integration with OKR generation (P2-05g). Session documentation was created to preserve architectural decisions and data model designs for future reference. The immediate next step launches P2-05a to implement the Prisma schema and database migration establishing the data foundation for the transformation tracking system.

# Transformation Session Schema Models Added to Prisma

Four new database models enable transformation initiative tracking with sessions, fields, variables, and conversational message history

The Prisma schema was extended with four interconnected models establishing the data foundation for P2-05 transformation initialization agent. TransformationSession serves as the root entity representing a transformation initiative conversation, storing userId, orgId, title, type (technical/organizational/business/hybrid), and status progression. TransformationField captures responses to the 12-14 orchestration form axes (problematique, objectifs_kpi, personas_volumes) with a unique constraint ensuring one value per axis per session, using @db.Text for potentially long textual responses and Json metadata for structured supplements. TransformationVariable models quantifiable metrics extracted during conversation, storing baseline (valueT0), target (valueTarget), and current (valueCurrent) values with optional units and categories, crucially including an optional keyResultId foreign key that bridges transformation tracking to the existing OKR system by linking variables to KeyResult records. TransformationMessage maintains complete conversational context with role-based message storage (user questions, assistant responses, system prompts) and Json metadata capturing which persona was active and which axes were covered. The schema design supports both the initialization workflow (P2-05) through T0/target value capture and the future documentary analysis workflow (P2-06) through valueCurrent updates. # P2-05a Supabase Migration SQL Created with RLS Policies and Audit Trail

Complete PostgreSQL migration script implements 4 transformation tables with indexes, triggers, Row Level Security policies, and append-only message history

A comprehensive PostgreSQL migration script was created for P2-05a implementing the transformation session data layer with enterprise-grade security and performance features. The script establishes four interconnected tables following Supabase conventions with snake_case naming and timestamptz columns. The transformation_sessions table serves as the root entity with user and organization foreign keys, transformation type classification, and lifecycle status tracking, indexed on three dimensions (user, org, status) for optimal query performance across common access patterns. transformation_fields stores axis-specific textual data with a unique constraint preventing duplicate axes per session, while transformation_variables tracks quantifiable metrics with T0 baseline, target, and current values plus optional KeyResult linkage for OKR integration. The transformation_messages table maintains complete conversation history with role-based attribution and JSONB metadata capturing contextual information like active persona and covered axes. Automatic timestamp management leverages PostgreSQL's trigger system with a reusable update_updated_at_column() function applied to the three mutable tables (sessions, fields, variables), while messages remain timestamped only at creation for audit integrity. Row Level Security represents a critical security layer with 18 granular policies enforcing user ownership boundaries - users can only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE their own sessions, and access to child records (fields, variables, messages) is validated through subqueries checking parent session ownership. This multi-tenant security model ensures complete data isolation between users without application-layer enforcement. The messages table implements append-only semantics with no UPDATE or DELETE policies, preserving complete conversation history for compliance, debugging, and model improvement - this immutability prevents tampering with audit trails while still allowing users to view and create their own messages. The script uses CREATE IF NOT EXISTS and CREATE OR REPLACE patterns enabling safe repeated execution, and JSONB columns provide schema flexibility for storing structured metadata without rigid column definitions. The optional key_result_id foreign key on transformation_variables creates the crucial linkage enabling automated OKR generation and bidirectional synchronization between transformation tracking and traditional OKR management.

# Database Migration Failed Due to UUID vs TEXT Type Mismatch in Foreign Keys

Supabase SQL editor reported incompatible types error for user_id and org_id foreign key constraints requiring TEXT to UUID conversion

The P2-05a database migration execution in Supabase SQL editor failed with a foreign key constraint error revealing a critical type mismatch in the migration script. The transformation_sessions table was created with user_id and org_id columns defined as TEXT type, but these columns reference the users.id and organizations.id columns which are UUID type in the existing database schema. PostgreSQL's strict type checking prevents foreign key relationships between incompatible types, correctly rejecting the constraint creation. This error indicates the migration SQL file was generated without properly inspecting the actual database column types - while the Prisma schema correctly specifies @id @default(uuid()) for User and Organization models, the SQL CREATE TABLE statements used TEXT instead of UUID for the foreign key columns. The same type mismatch likely affects the transformation_variables table's key_result_id column since KeyResult also uses UUID for its primary key. This is a common gotcha when manually writing SQL migrations for Prisma schemas - the Prisma type String maps to TEXT in PostgreSQL, but UUID fields require explicit UUID type in SQL even though Prisma represents them as String in the schema. The fix requires updating all foreign key columns (user_id, org_id, key_result_id) from TEXT to UUID type in the migration SQL file to match the referenced tables' primary key types.

# Fixed Foreign Key Type Mismatch in Transformation Sessions Migration

Changed user_id and org_id from UUID to TEXT in transformation_sessions table to match existing schema string-based identifiers

A type mismatch error was fixed in the P2-05a transformation migration SQL file. The initial migration defined user_id and org_id columns as UUID type with foreign key constraints to users(id) and organizations(id), but the existing Prisma schema defines these primary keys as String type with uuid() default values, not native PostgreSQL UUID type. This mismatch would cause the migration to fail with foreign key constraint errors because PostgreSQL requires exact type matching between foreign key columns and their referenced primary keys. The fix changed both user_id and org_id from "UUID NOT NULL" to "TEXT NOT NULL" to align with the string-based UUID implementation used throughout the existing schema. This is a common pattern when using ORMs like Prisma that store UUIDs as strings rather than native PostgreSQL UUID types, providing flexibility while maintaining uniqueness guarantees. The RLS policies at the end of the migration already correctly cast auth.uid()::text to match the TEXT type, indicating the string-based approach was the intended design. This fix ensures the transformation_sessions table can properly establish foreign key relationships with the users and organizations tables without type conversion errors.

The Prisma schema provides a complete data model for the transfo-ia-okr platform combining traditional OKR management with AI-powered transformation tracking. The schema's relational integrity is enforced through foreign keys with cascading deletes, and indexes optimize common query patterns like fetching all sessions for a user or all variables for a session. This foundation supports the P2-05b next task which will create TypeScript types mirroring these Prisma models.

The transfo-ia-okr project implements a sophisticated AI agent configuration system centered around mandatory auto-activation rules. The task management protocol reads .taskmaster/TASKS/tasks-ralph.md to identify current tasks by status and priority, verify dependencies, generate ralph-loop commands, and update task status automatically.

Session management enforces strict lifecycle rules: sc:load at startup reads PROJECT_CONTEXT.md and latest SESSION_*.md files, periodic checkpoints save context every 30 minutes using claude-mem MCP, and sc:save at session end persists all context. # Comprehensive TypeScript Type System for Transformation Agent Implemented

Complete type definitions for transformation sessions with 4 enums, 40 axes across 3 domains, metadata structures, DTOs, and utility functions totaling 858 lines

The src/types/transformation.ts file implements a comprehensive TypeScript type system for the P2-05 transformation agent feature, providing 858 lines of carefully structured type definitions, interfaces, DTOs, and utility functions that serve as the contract layer between the frontend UI, API routes, database layer, and AI conversation engine.

The type system begins with four foundational enums establishing the domain vocabulary. TransformationType defines the four transformation categories (TECHNICAL, ORGANIZATIONAL, BUSINESS, HYBRID) that the router AI will detect from user input. TransformationSessionStatus tracks the lifecycle stages (draft for new sessions, in_progress during conversation, completed when all required axes collected and variables extracted, archived for historical sessions). ChatRole distinguishes message origins (user, assistant, system) in the conversation history. VariableCategory provides eight classification buckets (performance, quality, adoption, risk, financial, operational, satisfaction, efficiency) for organizing extracted measurable variables.

The axis definitions translate the FORMULAIRES - Orchestration.txt framework into code with three parallel structures. TechnicalAxis enumerates 12 technical documentation points matching the reference document, OrganizationalAxis defines 14 organizational change dimensions, and BusinessAxis specifies 14 business/customer-focused aspects. Each axis set includes complete metadata arrays (TECHNICAL_AXES_METADATA, ORGANIZATIONAL_AXES_METADATA, BUSINESS_AXES_METADATA) containing structured information for each axis: a unique key identifier, a human-readable French label, a detailed description explaining what information to capture, a required boolean flag (typically 9-10 required axes per type), and an order number for sequential presentation. For example, TechnicalAxis.OBJECTIFS_KPI has description "Traduire les objectifs business en indicateurs de performance technique (SLO/SLA)" with required=true and order=2, while QUESTIONS_OUVERTES has required=false and order=10.

The base interfaces model the four Prisma entities created in P2-05a. TransformationSession represents the overall transformation initiative with userId and orgId for multi-tenancy, title for user-friendly identification, type enum, status enum, and timestamps. TransformationField stores individual axis responses with sessionId foreign key, axis string identifier, value containing the text response, and metadata JSON object capturing completion timestamp, confidence score, and array of extractedVariables linked to this field. TransformationVariable models the critical measurable metrics with name and optional description, category classification, the three numeric values (valueT0 baseline, valueTarget goal, valueCurrent tracking), optional unit string (%, ms, €), and optional keyResultId for OKR linkage. TransformationMessage preserves conversation history with role enum, content text, and metadata JSON containing persona identifier (tech/orga/metier/router), axesCovered string array, variablesExtracted array, and confidence score.

Extended interfaces support complex query patterns. SessionWithFields adds fields array for displaying collected context, SessionWithVariables adds variables array for showing extracted metrics, SessionWithMessages adds messages array for conversation replay, SessionFull combines all three for complete session hydration, and VariableWithKeyResult includes denormalized KeyResult details (id, title, currentValue, targetValue) for dashboard displays without additional queries.

The DTO layer provides clean API contracts. Create inputs accept only necessary fields: CreateTransformationSessionInput requires title and type with optional initialDescription for router analysis, CreateFieldInput needs sessionId/axis/value with optional metadata, CreateVariableInput specifies sessionId/name/valueT0/valueTarget with optional description/category/unit, and CreateMessageInput takes sessionId/role/content with optional metadata. Update inputs use Partial types allowing selective field updates: UpdateSessionInput permits title, type, or status changes, UpdateFieldInput allows value or metadata refinement, UpdateVariableInput supports updating any field including valueCurrent progression or keyResultId linkage. Response types add computed data: SessionResponse combines session entity with calculated TransformationProgress (totalAxes, completedAxes, percentComplete, totalVariables, variablesWithKeyResults), while SessionListItem provides summary fields for list views.

Chat API types enable the streaming conversation interface. ChatRequest contains sessionId context and user message text. ChatResponse returns the assistant's TransformationMessage plus optional metadata: detectedType if router classified the transformation, axesCovered array showing which documentation points were addressed, variablesExtracted array with newly identified metrics, suggestedNextAxis recommendation for conversation flow, and sessionProgress summary. ChatStreamEvent supports server-sent events with five type discriminators: 'text' for incremental response streaming, 'metadata' for conversation annotations, 'variable' for real-time variable extraction, 'complete' for stream termination, and 'error' for exception handling.

Router and persona types orchestrate the AI conversation engine. RouterResult captures the initial classification with detected TransformationType, confidence score (0-1), reasoning explanation, and suggestedPersona recommendation (tech/orga/metier). PersonaContext provides the conversation agent with full session state: sessionType for persona selection, completedAxes array for progress tracking, pendingAxes array for next question selection, currentAxis for focused questioning, extractedVariables history for context, and conversationHistory for continuity. ExtractedVariableRaw represents parser output with name, description, valueT0, valueTarget, unit, category, confidence score, and sourceText provenance. VariableExtractionResult aggregates extraction attempts with variables array, axisCompleted flag, and suggestedNextQuestions for conversation continuation.

Type guards enable runtime validation and type narrowing for API input sanitization. Four guards check enum membership: isTransformationType, isTransformationSessionStatus, isChatRole, and isVariableCategory, each validating the input is a string matching one of the enum values.

Utility functions implement core business logic. calculateSessionProgress computes completion percentage by counting completed required axes versus total required axes for the session type. getNextPendingAxis returns the first incomplete required axis by order number, guiding conversation flow. canCompleteSession validates completion criteria returning an object with canComplete boolean (true when all required axes done and at least one variable extracted), missingAxes string array for user feedback, and missingVariables boolean flag. Three format functions provide French display labels: formatTransformationType maps TECHNICAL→"Technique", formatSessionStatus maps IN_PROGRESS→"En cours", formatVariableCategory maps PERFORMANCE→"Performance". The getAxesMetadataByType function handles the HYBRID case specially by merging unique axes from all three domain metadata arrays into a deduplicated sorted collection, supporting multi-domain transformations that span technical, organizational, and business concerns simultaneously.

# Existing OKR Suggestions Prompt System Discovered

okr-suggestions.ts provides reference pattern for transformation prompts with system prompts, context builders, and JSON response parsing

The existing src/lib/ai/prompts/okr-suggestions.ts file provides a proven reference pattern that can guide the implementation of P2-05c transformation prompts. This file implements the P2-04 AI-powered suggestions feature using Google Gemini API, demonstrating effective prompt engineering techniques that should be adapted for the transformation agent.

The prompt system establishes a layered architecture starting with SYSTEM_PROMPT_OKR_EXPERT defining the base AI persona as an OKR expert with 15+ years of experience in agile and digital transformation, expertise covering John Doerr's OKR methodology, SMART objective definition best practices, cross-team strategic alignment, and performance measurement with key indicators. This base prompt includes response rules enforcing French language output, concise actionable advice, concrete examples when relevant, bullet-point structure for readability, and professional yet accessible tone. Two specialized system prompts extend the base: SYSTEM_PROMPT_OBJECTIVE_IMPROVEMENT adds mission-specific guidance for improving objective formulations with criteria that objectives should be inspiring and ambitious, qualitative without metrics, time-bounded to specific periods, strategically aligned, and universally comprehensible; SYSTEM_PROMPT_KEY_RESULTS_GENERATION focuses on suggesting measurable key results with criteria including clear metrics, ambitious but achievable targets (70-80% success rate), time constraints, direct linkage to parent objective, and independence from other KRs.

Context interfaces define strongly-typed input data structures. ObjectiveContext captures title, optional description, period string, optional teamName, and optional existingKeyResults array containing previously defined KRs to avoid duplication. KeyResultContext includes objectiveTitle for parent context, KR title and description, metricType enum (percentage/number/currency/boolean), and three numeric values (startValue baseline, targetValue goal, currentValue current progress).

Three prompt builder functions demonstrate the pattern for generating dynamic user prompts from context. buildObjectiveImprovementPrompt constructs a multi-line prompt string starting with "Objectif à améliorer:" followed by title, conditionally including description if provided, period specification, optional team name, and if existingKeyResults array is populated, a numbered list of current KRs with their targets and metric types, concluding with "Analyse cet objectif et propose des améliorations." buildKeyResultsSuggestionPrompt follows similar structure but ends with explicit JSON format specification defining the expected response schema with keyResults array containing title, description, metricType enum, startValue, targetValue, and justification fields. buildKeyResultImprovementPrompt focuses on single KR improvement analyzing formulation, target ambition (balancing ambition with achievability), and parent objective alignment.

Response parsing demonstrates robust extraction and validation. parseKeyResultsSuggestion function handles Gemini's potentially non-pure JSON responses by using regex pattern /\{[\s\S]*"keyResults"[\s\S]*\}/ to extract JSON from surrounding text, parsing with JSON.parse wrapped in try-catch, validating the keyResults array exists, then mapping each element to normalize fields with String() coercion for text fields, conditional description and justification inclusion, validateMetricType validation with 'percentage' fallback default, and Number() coercion with || 0 and || 100 defaults for numeric values. The validateMetricType helper checks if the type string is in the validTypes array ['percentage', 'number', 'currency', 'boolean'] before casting, preventing invalid metric types from propagating.

This pattern provides clear guidance for P2-05c implementation: transformation prompts should similarly define base persona system prompts (transformation router expert, technical transformation expert, organizational change expert, business transformation expert), create context interfaces capturing session state (completed axes, pending axes, current axis focus, extracted variables, conversation history), implement builder functions generating dynamic user prompts based on context (buildRouterDetectionPrompt, buildTechnicalAxisQuestionPrompt, buildOrganizationalAxisQuestionPrompt, buildBusinessAxisQuestionPrompt, buildVariableExtractionPrompt), specify JSON response formats in prompts for structured extraction, and implement parsing functions with regex extraction, validation, and normalization to handle Gemini's text-embedded JSON responses robustly.

The primary session agent created task #1 to implement the transformation router prompt system, representing the first concrete step in executing P2-05c (Prompts IA). # Task Created for Variable Extraction Prompt Implementation

Agent initiated task to create variable-extractor.ts for converting conversational responses into measurable variables with T0, target values, and confidence scoring

Task #5 addresses the critical variable extraction component of the transformation agent system, implementing the core mechanism that transforms qualitative conversational input into quantitative measurable variables suitable for OKR tracking and dashboard visualization. The variable-extractor.ts file will contain prompts enabling the AI to parse user responses and identify numerical metrics with baseline and target values.

This extractor fulfills the architectural requirement clarified in memory observation #896 where the user emphasized that the application's core objective is measuring impact of each mission action and tracking evolution of indicators, curves, progressions, and OKRs over time. The transformation conversations (whether technical, organizational, or business) must produce measurable variables that can be quantitatively tracked, similar to the INIT1.md model examples like adoption_rate, trust_index, proof_density, quality_stability, value_perceived, risk_perceived, and effort_to_try.

The extractor will analyze text responses from axis questions and generate ExtractedVariableRaw objects containing: name (concise variable identifier), description (explanation of what is measured), valueT0 (current baseline numeric value representing the starting point), valueTarget (desired goal numeric value defining success), unit (measurement unit like %, ms, €, or dimensionless), category (classification into one of 8 VariableCategory enums: performance, quality, adoption, risk, financial, operational, satisfaction, efficiency), confidence (0-1 score indicating extraction certainty), and sourceText (original text snippet providing traceability).

The prompt must handle diverse transformation types extracting technical variables (latency metrics in milliseconds, availability percentages, test coverage ratios, deployment frequency), organizational variables (eNPS scores, time-to-market reductions in days/weeks, adoption rates, training completion percentages), and business variables (NPS deltas, revenue growth percentages, conversion rate improvements, support cost reduction percentages). The extractor operates after each significant conversation turn, accumulating variables throughout the session that will eventually link to KeyResult entities via the TransformationVariable.keyResultId field, enabling automated OKR generation from the collected transformation context.

# Risk Analysis Prompts System for OKR Assessment Discovered

risk-analysis.ts implements AI-powered risk evaluation with 4-level scoring, factor analysis, and actionable recommendations for OKR tracking

The src/lib/ai/prompts/risk-analysis.ts file demonstrates advanced prompt engineering for complex analytical tasks, providing another reference pattern for the P2-05c transformation prompts implementation. This file extends the base SYSTEM_PROMPT_OKR_EXPERT persona with specialized risk analysis capabilities, showing how to layer domain-specific expertise onto foundational AI character definitions.

The risk analyst system prompt defines a comprehensive evaluation framework assessing five key risk factors: progression relative to time elapsed (comparing actual progress percentage against time progress percentage to identify gaps), recent trend direction (improvement or degradation over recent check-ins), check-in confidence levels (team certainty in reported values on 1-5 scale), current-target gap magnitude (distance from goal), and complexity with dependencies (inherent difficulty and external blockers). This multi-factor assessment produces a four-level risk classification scheme with clear thresholds and visual indicators: low risk (green) indicates on-track progression conforming to expectations, moderate risk (yellow) signals slight delays requiring attention, high risk (orange) marks significant delays necessitating corrective actions, and critical risk (red) identifies compromised objectives recommending escalation to stakeholders.

The RiskAnalysisContext interface demonstrates comprehensive context capture for analytical prompts, combining objective-level metadata (title, description, period bounds, start/end dates, current status) with detailed key result arrays containing full metric state (title, type, value trilogy of start/target/current, calculated progress percentage, optional lastCheckInDate for recency, optional lastConfidence score, optional trend enum), plus aggregated metrics (overallProgress across all KRs, daysElapsed and daysTotal for temporal context, calculated timeProgress percentage). This rich context enables sophisticated gap analysis comparing expected progress (time elapsed percentage) against actual progress (achievement percentage) at both objective and individual KR levels.

The buildRiskAnalysisPrompt function showcases advanced prompt construction with calculated fields and conditional formatting. It computes progressGap as timeProgress minus overallProgress showing whether the objective is ahead (negative gap) or behind (positive gap) schedule, then constructs a detailed multi-section prompt presenting objective metadata, temporal progression metrics with absolute and percentage values, overall progress with gap calculation and sign formatting, and per-KR details including metric type, progress with current/target values, individual KR gaps, conditional trend arrows (↑ en hausse, ↓ en baisse, → stable), and conditional confidence scores. The prompt concludes with explicit JSON response format specification defining the expected RiskAnalysisResult structure, guiding the AI to produce parseable structured output.

The buildQuickRecommendationsPrompt demonstrates lightweight alternative prompting for rapid feedback scenarios, calculating the single progressGap, formatting concise context (objective title, progress vs time, gap with sign, optional at-risk KR list), and requesting exactly 3 concrete actionable recommendations in one sentence each formatted as numbered list. This dual-prompt approach (comprehensive analysis vs quick recommendations) shows how to offer different depth/speed tradeoffs for various user scenarios.

Response parsing functions implement robust extraction and validation. parseRiskAnalysis uses regex pattern /\{[\s\S]*"riskLevel"[\s\S]*\}/ to locate JSON within surrounding text, validates presence of required riskLevel and summary fields, normalizes riskLevel to one of four valid enum values defaulting to 'moderate' if invalid, clamps score to 0-100 range with 50 default for missing/invalid values, and ensures factors, recommendations, and keyMetricsToWatch are arrays (empty arrays if missing/invalid). parseQuickRecommendations demonstrates simpler text parsing using regex /^\d+\.\s*(.+)/ to extract numbered list items, trimming whitespace, and limiting results to maximum 5 recommendations preventing over-verbose responses.

This risk-analysis.ts file provides valuable patterns for P2-05c transformation prompts: system prompts should extend base personas with specialized mission statements and evaluation frameworks, context interfaces should capture comprehensive state enabling sophisticated analysis, prompt builders should perform calculations and gap analysis within prompt construction, explicit JSON format specifications guide AI toward parseable structured responses, dual-prompt approaches offer depth/speed tradeoffs, and parser functions should robustly handle malformed responses with regex extraction, validation, normalization, and sensible defaults. The transformation router and variable extractor can adopt these proven techniques for reliable structured output from Gemini API.
