# Streaming Chat API Route Implemented with SSE and Persona Orchestration

691-line POST /api/ai/chat endpoint implementing Server-Sent Events streaming with router classification, three-persona system, automatic variable extraction, and database persistence

The streaming chat API route at src/app/api/ai/chat/route.ts delivers the complete backend infrastructure for P2-05e transformation conversations implementing Server-Sent Events streaming with sophisticated persona orchestration and automatic variable extraction across 691 lines. The implementation begins with rate limiting using an in-memory Map tracking request counts per IP address with 60-second sliding windows enforcing a maximum of 20 requests per minute, higher than the 10 request limit for /api/ai/suggest reflecting the conversational nature where users may send multiple clarifying messages rapidly. The core generateChatStream async generator function orchestrates the entire conversation lifecycle starting by loading the full session context with getTransformationSessionFull retrieving fields, variables, and message history in a single query, immediately saving the user message via createTransformationMessage establishing persistence before AI processing begins. First message detection triggers router classification: when session status is draft and message count is 1 or less, the system attempts quickClassify keyword-based analysis accepting results with confidence ≥0.7 to minimize latency, falling back to AI-powered classification via buildRouterPrompt with SYSTEM_PROMPT_TRANSFORMATION_ROUTER when confidence is insufficient, gracefully handling API failures by reverting to quick classification results, then updating session type and status to in_progress via updateTransformationSession and yielding type_detected metadata event before streaming the persona introduction message generated by getIntroMessage and persisted with isIntro metadata flag. Persona selection maps transformation types to specialized experts: TECHNICAL routes to persona-tech with 12 technical axes, ORGANIZATIONAL routes to persona-orga with 14 change management axes, BUSINESS routes to persona-metier with 14 market-focused axes, and HYBRID defaults to tech initially enabling later transitions. Current axis determination calls getNextAxis which delegates to type-specific functions (getNextTechnicalAxis, getNextOrganizationalAxis, getNextBusinessAxis) returning the first uncompleted required axis or null when collection is complete, with HYBRID type attempting tech axes first, then organizational, then business providing comprehensive coverage. PersonaContext construction aggregates session type, completed axes from field records, pending axes by filtering total axes against completed set, current axis identifier, extracted variables array, and full conversation history enabling context-aware prompt generation. Prompt construction distinguishes between active collection and completion modes: when currentAxis exists, buildAxisPrompt routes to persona-specific builders (buildTechAxisQuestionPrompt, buildOrgaAxisQuestionPrompt, buildMetierAxisQuestionPrompt) passing axis identifier, PersonaContext, and previous user responses from last 3 messages, then appending recent conversation context from last 10 messages and current user message with structured instructions to analyze user input, identify information relevant to current axis, pose 1-2 follow-up questions, and maintain conversational encouraging tone; when all axes are completed, the prompt shifts to summary mode congratulating completion, offering to review points, and suggesting OKR generation transition. Response streaming iterates generateContentStream from Gemini with 1500 max output tokens and 0.7 temperature accumulating chunks into fullResponse while yielding text events via formatSSEEvent which formats ChatStreamEvent objects as data: {JSON}\n\n following SSE specification, catching streaming errors to yield error events before returning. Message persistence saves the complete assistant response with metadata tracking persona, current axis, and axes covered array enabling conversation replay and context reconstruction. Variable extraction activates when responses exceed 100 characters and an axis is active, first attempting quickExtractVariables pattern-based extraction against combined user message and assistant response, then for user messages over 50 characters invoking AI extraction via buildVariableExtractionPrompt with session type, axis context, conversation text, and previous variables to avoid duplication, parsing responses with parseExtractionResponse yielding VariableExtractionResult with variables array and axisCompleted boolean triggering upsertTransformationField to mark axis completion with completedAt timestamp and extracted variable names in metadata. Variable persistence iterates extracted variables checking existence by name, filtering by confidence threshold ≥0.5, saving via createTransformationVariable, and yielding variable events with complete TransformationVariable records enabling real-time UI updates as metrics materialize during conversation. Progress calculation retrieves updated completed axes via getCompletedAxes, computes percentage against total axes from type-specific metadata, determines next axis, and yields complete event with message ID, progress percentage, axis counts, and next axis identifier providing clients with comprehensive completion context. The POST handler validates availability with isGeminiAvailable returning 503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE when GOOGLE_AI_API_KEY is missing, enforces rate limits returning 429 TOO_MANY_REQUESTS with French error message when exceeded, parses and validates request body with chatRequestSchema.safeParse returning 400 BAD_REQUEST with flattened validation errors when validation fails, verifies session existence returning 404 NOT_FOUND when session is missing, creates ReadableStream with start controller iterating generateChatStream chunks enqueuing each into the stream and catching errors to emit error events before closing, and returns Response wrapping stream with SSE headers including Content-Type text/event-stream, Cache-Control no-cache preventing caching, Connection keep-alive maintaining persistent connection, and X-Accel-Buffering no disabling nginx buffering for immediate chunk delivery. Helper functions provide reusable logic: getPersonaSystemPrompt maps persona types to appropriate system prompts, getPersonaFromType converts transformation types to persona identifiers, getIntroMessage generates persona-specific introduction messages, getNextAxis handles type-specific axis progression including HYBRID cascading logic, buildAxisPrompt routes to persona-specific prompt builders with proper type assertions, and formatSSEEvent ensures consistent SSE event formatting. Error handling provides graceful degradation across multiple failure modes: session not found yields error event and returns early, streaming errors log to console and yield error events, variable extraction failures log errors but continue conversation flow avoiding interruption, database write errors log but don't block streaming, and top-level exceptions return 500 INTERNAL_ERROR responses. The complementary GET handler provides health check returning availability status, service identifier, and endpoint documentation. This comprehensive implementation delivers production-ready streaming chat infrastructure orchestrating router classification, persona-driven conversations, real-time variable extraction, persistent message storage, and progressive UI updates through Server-Sent Events enabling natural conversational experiences while systematically collecting structured transformation data across technical, organizational, and business dimensions.

# React Chat Stream Hook Implemented with SSE Consumption and State Management

456-line useChatStream hook providing message state, ReadableStream processing, event parsing, abort handling, and callback system for real-time chat integration

The useChatStream React hook at src/hooks/use-chat-stream.ts provides comprehensive client-side infrastructure for consuming Server-Sent Events from the /api/ai/chat endpoint across 456 lines implementing state management, stream processing, event parsing, and error handling. The hook's public interface accepts UseChatStreamOptions specifying sessionId for conversation context plus five optional callbacks enabling reactive UI updates: onMessage triggered when assistant messages complete, onVariable triggered when new metrics are extracted, onTypeDetected triggered when router classifies transformation type, onError triggered on failures, and onComplete triggered with progress updates. Internal ChatState management maintains messages array of ChatMessage records with id, role (user/assistant/system), content text, timestamp, and optional metadata tracking persona, currentAxis, axisLabel, isIntro flag, and isStreaming status; variables array collecting TransformationVariable records as they're extracted; boolean flags isLoading indicating network activity and isStreaming indicating active content reception; error string for failure messages; detectedType storing TransformationType once classified; currentAxis tracking conversation focus; and progress holding TransformationProgress with axis counts and completion percentage. Three refs provide stable storage across renders: abortControllerRef holds AbortController for stream cancellation, lastMessageRef stores last sent message enabling retry, and streamingMessageIdRef tracks the assistant message being updated during streaming. The useEffect cleanup hook ensures abortController.abort() is called on unmount preventing memory leaks from abandoned streams. The core sendMessage function implements comprehensive request handling: validating message is non-empty and not already loading, calling abortStream to cancel any existing stream, creating ChatMessage for user input with generated ID and timestamp, storing message text in lastMessageRef for retry, adding user message to state while setting isLoading true, creating fresh AbortController, initiating fetch to /api/ai/chat with POST method, Content-Type application/json header, JSON body containing sessionId and message, and signal from AbortController for cancellation, throwing descriptive errors if response is not ok or body is missing, creating streaming message placeholder with empty content and isStreaming metadata, setting isStreaming true in state, obtaining ReadableStream reader from response.body, initializing TextDecoder for UTF-8 conversion, maintaining buffer string for incomplete lines and accumulatedContent string for full response, entering read loop calling reader.read() for { done, value } tuples, decoding Uint8Array values appending to buffer, splitting buffer on newlines keeping last incomplete segment, filtering empty lines and comment lines starting with colon, parsing each line via parseSSEEvent extracting JSON from data: prefix with try-catch error suppression, switching on event.type to handle five cases. Text events accumulate event.content into accumulatedContent and update the streaming message's content property via setState mapping messages array to replace matching message ID, providing real-time content updates creating typewriter effect. Metadata events extract multiple properties: detectedType updates state and triggers onTypeDetected callback when router classifies type, currentAxis updates state tracking conversation focus, persona updates streaming message metadata with persona identifier plus currentAxis and axisLabel for context display. Variable events extract event.variable appending to state variables array and triggering onVariable callback enabling immediate UI updates as metrics materialize. Complete events construct TransformationProgress from metadata properties (totalAxes, completedAxes, progress percentage) updating state and triggering onComplete callback. Error events throw Error with event.error message caught by outer catch block. After read loop completes, finalization updates state setting isLoading and isStreaming false, updating streaming message with final accumulatedContent and isStreaming false metadata, constructing final ChatMessage, calling onMessage callback, and clearing streamingMessageIdRef. The catch block distinguishes AbortError (from manual cancellation) returning silently versus real errors extracting message, updating state with error, calling onError callback, and removing streaming message placeholder if present. The finally block clears abortControllerRef regardless of outcome. The retry function checks lastMessageRef for stored message, removes last user message from state (handling edge case where error occurred before assistant response), clears error, and calls sendMessage with stored message enabling one-click error recovery. Additional action methods include clearError resetting error state, clearChat calling abortStream then resetting all state to initial values, and abortStream aborting controller and updating loading flags. Helper functions provide utilities: generateMessageId creates unique identifiers combining millisecond timestamp with 7-character random string from base36 encoding, and parseSSEEvent safely parses SSE data: lines extracting JSON with try-catch suppressing parse errors and filtering [DONE] sentinel and empty strings. The return object exposes eight state properties (messages, variables, isLoading, isStreaming, error, detectedType, currentAxis, progress) and five action methods (sendMessage, clearChat, clearError, retry, abortStream) providing complete programmatic control over chat lifecycle. This hook abstracts the complexity of SSE consumption, incremental content updates, event discrimination, abort handling, and error recovery into a clean React API enabling chat UI components to focus on presentation logic while the hook manages streaming infrastructure, state transitions, and network resilience.

# ChatMessage Component Created with Markdown Support and Message Grouping

Speech bubble message component with persona labels, streaming indicators, inline markdown formatting, and intelligent message grouping logic

The ChatMessage component was created to render individual conversation messages with comprehensive styling and formatting capabilities. The component accepts ChatMessageType from use-chat-stream hook and renders with role-based layout variations: user messages align right with flex-row-reverse using primary color backgrounds, while assistant messages align left with flex-row using muted backgrounds with semi-transparent borders. The avatar system provides visual role identification with user avatars displaying solid primary colored circles containing User icon (h-8 w-8), and assistant avatars showing gradient Bot icon (from-primary/20 via-primary/10 to-transparent) with ring border, plus absolute-positioned ping animation indicator (2.5x2.5 with animate-ping) when message is streaming. Persona awareness is implemented through PERSONA_CONFIG mapping four persona types to French labels and color schemes: tech persona shows "Expert Technique" in blue (text-blue-600 dark:text-blue-400), orga shows "Expert Organisation" in violet, metier shows "Expert Métier" in emerald, and router shows "Analyse" in amber. The component displays optional persona label above message bubble and optional axis label from metadata for context tracking. Message bubble styling creates speech bubble appearance through rounded-2xl base with directional cuts: user messages use rounded-tr-md creating top-right notch, assistant messages use rounded-tl-md creating top-left notch. The MessageContent sub-component implements inline markdown formatting using React.useMemo for performance, processing content line-by-line to handle paragraph breaks (empty lines become br tags) and applying regex transformations for three formatting types: bold uses **text** or __text__ converted to strong tags, italic uses single *text* or _text_ with negative lookahead/lookbehind to avoid matching double asterisks converted to em tags, and inline code uses `code` backticks converted to code tags with monospace styling. The processed HTML is rendered using dangerouslySetInnerHTML (safe since transformations are controlled) with Tailwind CSS descendant selectors styling nested elements: [&>strong]:font-semibold, [&>em]:italic, [&>code]:rounded with background colors and padding. Streaming state handling includes inline StreamingIndicator cursor (ml-0.5 inline-block align-middle) appearing after content during active streaming, "..." muted placeholder when streaming with no content yet, and hiding timestamps during streaming. Timestamps use date-fns formatDistanceToNow with French locale providing relative time strings like "il y a 5 minutes". The ChatMessageGroup companion component provides intelligent message grouping logic by iterating through messages array and creating groups of consecutive messages from the same role, reducing visual clutter by showing avatars only on first message of each group and timestamps only on last message, with reduced gap (gap-1.5) between grouped messages versus larger gap (gap-4) between different role groups. Animation support includes animate-in fade-in-0 slide-in-from-bottom-2 duration-300 for smooth message entry, applied only to latest message in groups.

# TypeScript Error Root Cause Identified in Generator Return Type

generateChatStream declares AsyncGenerator<string> but yields Uint8Array from encoder.encode calls causing type mismatch

The TypeScript type checking errors stem from a mismatch between the generateChatStream generator's declared return type and its actual yield values. The function signature declares AsyncGenerator<string, void, unknown> indicating it will yield string values, but the implementation creates a TextEncoder instance at the start and consistently yields encoder.encode(formatSSEEvent(...)) which returns Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer> not strings. The formatSSEEvent helper correctly returns string formatted as SSE events with data: prefix and double newline terminators, but the encoder.encode() wrapper converts these strings to Uint8Array binary data. The ReadableStream controller.enqueue method in the POST handler expects Uint8Array chunks for binary streaming. The fix requires either changing the generator signature to AsyncGenerator<Uint8Array, void, unknown> to match actual yields, or removing encoder.encode calls and having the ReadableStream controller handle encoding, or yielding strings and encoding in the controller. The most consistent approach is changing the generator type to match the Uint8Array yields since SSE binary streaming is more robust than string streaming.

Faits: ["generateChatStream function signature declares AsyncGenerator<string, void, unknown> expecting string yields","Function creates TextEncoder instance then calls encoder.encode() which returns Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>","All yield statements pass encoder.encode(formatSSEEvent(...)) yielding Uint8Array instead of string causing 11 TypeScript errors","formatSSEEvent helper function returns string with data: prefix and double newline for SSE format","ReadableStream controller.enqueue expects Uint8Array chunks for binary streaming but generator type signature promises strings"]
summary: TypeScript Error Root Cause Identified in Generator Return Type

# ChatInput Component Created with Auto-Resize and Context-Aware Placeholders

Textarea input with automatic height adjustment, Enter/Shift+Enter shortcuts, abort button during streaming, and axis-specific placeholder text

The ChatInput component was created to provide the message input interface for the transformation chat with sophisticated UX features. The component implements automatic textarea height adjustment through adjustHeight callback that resets height to 'auto', calculates scrollHeight, and applies new height clamped between 44px minimum (single line) and 120px maximum (approximately 5 lines), triggered by useEffect on value changes ensuring smooth multi-line expansion. Keyboard interaction supports two modes: Enter without Shift triggers form submission via formRef.current.requestSubmit(), while Shift+Enter allows new line insertion, with visual hints displayed below the input showing kbd elements styled with monospace font and muted backgrounds explaining "Entrée pour envoyer, Maj+Entrée pour une nouvelle ligne". The component implements context-aware placeholder system through AXIS_PLACEHOLDERS configuration mapping axis keys to French prompts: problematique shows "Décrivez la problématique que vous souhaitez résoudre...", objectifs_kpi shows "Quels sont vos objectifs et indicateurs clés ?", with fallback to generic "Écrivez votre message..." when no axis provided. Button state management provides two distinct modes: during streaming the component renders StopCircle button with destructive color scheme (text-destructive hover:bg-destructive/10) calling onAbort callback to cancel generation, while normal mode shows Send button with conditional styling (primary colors when canSend is true, muted when disabled) displaying either Loader2 spinner during loading or Send icon. Focus management uses useEffect to automatically focus the textarea on mount and refocus after successful message submission when component is not in loading/streaming/disabled state, improving keyboard accessibility. Form submission handling in handleSubmit prevents default, trims input value, validates against loading/streaming/disabled states, calls onSend callback with trimmed message, clears value state, and resets textarea height to 'auto' for next message. The form container uses refined styling with rounded-2xl borders, semi-transparent background (bg-background/80), backdrop-blur-sm for glassmorphism, border-border/60 subtle borders, and focus-within pseudo-class applying focus ring effects (border-primary/40 and ring-2 ring-primary/10) creating smooth visual feedback. The textarea itself uses transparent background (bg-transparent) to inherit form background, resize-none to prevent manual resizing, scrollbar-thin with custom thumb colors for overflow, placeholder:text-muted-foreground/50 for subtle placeholder text, and focus:outline-none to rely on form-level focus styling. CharacterCount companion component calculates percentage of max characters (default 2000), determines warning states (isWarning at 80%, isDanger at 95%), and applies conditional text colors (text-destructive for danger, text-amber-500 for warning, text-muted-foreground/50 for normal) with tabular-nums for consistent number width, displaying formatted counts like "1,234/2,000". Accessibility includes ARIA labels on textarea ("Message") and buttons ("Envoyer le message", "Arrêter la génération"), ensuring screen reader compatibility.

# Native Multi-Agent Orchestration Architecture Decisions for Phase 3 Systemic Analysis

User defined parallelism strategy, streaming UX, flexible domain granularity, and prompt optimization approach for native N8N workflow migration

Architectural decisions were finalized for implementing the native multi-agent orchestration system within the transfo-ia-okr application, migrating the N8N "Unfix" Strategic Analysis Orchestrator workflow into Phase 3 functionality.

The parallelism strategy establishes a concurrency limit of 5 simultaneous Gemini API calls, architected as one call per domain to enable parallel execution across all five analysis domains (Design & Dépendances, Expérience & Identité, Flux Valeur & Stratégie, People & Croissance, Structure & Gouvernance) while controlling resource consumption and API rate limits.

The user experience design emphasizes progressive streaming for fluid interaction. When a systemic analysis workflow launches, the General Manager output renders immediately to the user interface, providing context and investigation tracks as the first-stage analysis completes. Subsequently, domain analyses from specialized agents appear incrementally as they complete, allowing users to consume analysis results in real-time rather than waiting for batch completion.

Domain granularity introduces user choice flexibility. Rather than forcing full analysis execution across all five domains, users can select analysis scope based on their needs: complete analysis engaging all domains, or targeted analysis of 1, 2, 3, or 4 specific domains. This granular control enables focused investigation of relevant strategic areas while reducing token consumption and execution time for narrower scopes.

The prompt migration strategy permits optimization during the translation from N8N JSON configuration to native implementation. While the original N8N workflow contains comprehensive system prompts for 32+ specialized agents, the implementation can reduce prompt size through compression, removal of redundant instructions, and template optimization, provided analysis quality and performance remain consistent.

# Phase 3 Core Requirements Finalized: Conditional Synthesis, Database Prompts, Quota System, and Future RAG Integration

Five architectural decisions locked: conditional Chief Reporter synthesis, admin-modifiable database prompts, role-based quotas, deferred variable suggestions, and RAG system consideration

Five critical architectural decisions finalized the Phase 3 specification for N8N multi-agent orchestration integration into the transfo-ia-okr platform.

Decision 1 establishes conditional synthesis logic: when users select a single domain for analysis, the workflow terminates immediately after that domain's expert analysis completes, bypassing the Chief Reporter. When users select multiple domains (2-5), each domain's expert analysis outputs feed into the Chief Reporter (Rapporteur en Chef) who synthesizes N analyses into a unified systemic report. This optimization reduces API costs and latency for focused single-domain analyses while preserving comprehensive synthesis for multi-domain requests.

Decision 2 mandates database storage for all 39 agent prompts with administrative modification capabilities. This architectural choice prioritizes runtime configurability over version-controlled TypeScript files, enabling superadmin users to refine, optimize, or update agent prompts without requiring code deployments. The database approach supports prompt A/B testing, gradual rollouts of prompt improvements, and organization-specific prompt customization.

Decision 3 implements role-based quota enforcement: superadmin accounts receive unlimited systemic analysis invocations (open bar access), while normal user accounts are constrained to 2 complete systemic analyses per project maximum. This quota system balances API cost management (~40 Gemini Flash calls per full analysis) with user value delivery, preventing runaway costs while ensuring users can perform meaningful analyses. The per-project quota scope allows users to analyze multiple projects within their overall limit.

Decision 4 defers the variable suggestion feature to future development. The concept envisions systemic analyses identifying and suggesting complementary transformation variables to users based on expert insights, creating a feedback loop from analysis back to P2-05 variable qualification. This feature represents a future enhancement that would strengthen the connection between conversational qualification and deep systemic analysis.

Decision 5 introduces RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system consideration as a strategic architectural direction. The user recognizes that the platform will accumulate substantial domain knowledge across P2-05 conversational sessions, P3 systemic analyses from 39 experts, and standard OKR management activities. A RAG system would enable intelligent retrieval and reuse of this organizational knowledge, allowing future analyses to benefit from historical insights, patterns, and recommendations. This represents a potential Phase 4+ capability that would transform the platform from a transactional analysis tool into an organizational learning system with cumulative intelligence.

These decisions resolve the four open questions from the previous checkpoint and add the RAG consideration, enabling progression from P3 architectural design to implementation task execution. The conditional synthesis logic optimizes the critical path, database prompts enable runtime flexibility, quotas control costs, deferred features maintain scope discipline, and RAG planning establishes long-term vision.

# Phase 4 RAG System Data Source Analysis - Identifying Strategic Analysis Content for Indexing

Sequential thinking analysis identifies five data sources for RAG indexing: transformation sessions, systemic analysis outputs, domain syntheses, agent analyses, and final reports

The first thought in an 8-thought sequence established the foundation by cataloging content sources and estimating data volumes.

The RAG system will index five hierarchical layers of content produced by the transformation and strategic analysis pipeline. At the input layer, P2-05 TransformationSession data captures qualified transformation variables including project context, constraints, and objectives, generating 2-5 KB of JSON per session. This provides the initial problem framing that contextualizes subsequent analysis.

The strategic analysis pipeline produces four output layers. The General Manager's SystemicAnalysis output provides the initial structured analysis at 3-5 KB, establishing the analytical framework. Five domain synthesizers generate DomainAnalysis outputs covering Design & Dependencies, Experience & Identity, Value Flow & Strategy, People & Growth, and Structure & Governance, contributing 5-10 KB each for a domain layer total of 25-50 KB.

Each agent generates 3-8 KB of specialized analysis covering topics like Chaos Theory, Emergence, Causal Loop Diagrams, Agent-Based Modeling, System Archetypes, and others. This agent layer represents the core knowledge repository, totaling 96-256 KB per complete analysis cycle. A critical architectural question emerged regarding indexing granularity. The system must choose between indexing entire documents (preserving full context but reducing retrieval precision) versus chunking content into sections (improving retrieval relevance but risking context fragmentation). # Hybrid Chunking Strategy for RAG Document Indexation

Sequential thinking analysis recommends content-type-based chunking approach with semantic sections for agent analyses and whole documents for syntheses

A sequential thinking MCP analysis examined chunking and indexation granularity strategies for the RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) system that will index multi-agent analysis outputs. The analysis evaluated two primary approaches: storing entire documents versus breaking content into semantic sections.

Option A (whole document approach) offers simplicity and preserves full context but suffers from imprecise search capabilities and diluted embeddings that reduce retrieval relevance. Option B (semantic section approach) provides precision and relevance but introduces complexity and risks losing cross-section context.

The recommended solution adopts a hybrid approach tailored to content types. This strategy recognizes that different document types have different retrieval patterns and context requirements.

For transformation variables collected during P2-05 sessions, the strategy stores complete documents because these contain small volumes with tightly interconnected context that should remain unified for accurate retrieval.

General Manager analyses are chunked by semantic sections—specifically themes, risks, and investigation tracks (pistes). This sectioning aligns with the YAML structure produced by the General Manager agent and enables targeted queries like "show me all identified risks" or "what investigation tracks were generated for design domain."

Individual agent analyses (Chaos Theory Expert, Fractal Analysis, etc.) receive fine-grained chunking into three primary sections: resume_executif (executive summary), risques (risks), and recommandations (recommendations). This granular approach supports precise searches such as "what chaos theory risks were identified" or "recommendations from fractal analysis."

Domain synthesizers that perform meta-analysis across multiple expert reports are stored as whole documents because they already represent synthesized information and breaking them further would fragment the unified strategic vision they provide.

Final comprehensive reports are chunked by sections to allow targeted search within specific report segments while maintaining overall structure.

Each indexed chunk includes comprehensive metadata for filtering and retrieval: project_id and organization_id ensure multi-tenant data isolation, analysis_id provides traceability back to source analysis, domain and agent_type enable filtering by analysis domain or expert type, section_type categorizes the semantic purpose (resume, risque, recommandation, etc.), created_at provides temporal ordering, tokens_count tracks content size, and embedding stores the vector representation with 1536 dimensions compatible with OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 or Google Gemini embedding models.

This hybrid chunking strategy optimizes the trade-off between context preservation and retrieval precision by matching chunking granularity to content characteristics and expected query patterns. The approach enables both broad contextual searches and precise targeted queries while maintaining multi-tenant isolation and full traceability.

The sequential thinking process is at thought 2 of 8, indicating this chunking strategy decision is part of a larger ongoing architectural analysis of the RAG system implementation.

# Prisma Schema Design for RAG Knowledge Chunks with Supabase pgvector Integration

KnowledgeChunk model designed with multi-tenant support, source tracking, pgvector embeddings, and metadata for RAG-based systemic analysis retrieval

A Prisma schema was designed for the KnowledgeChunk model to support RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) functionality in the Phase 3 systemic analysis system, enabling semantic search across analysis outputs from the multi-agent orchestration workflow.

The schema implements comprehensive multi-tenancy through organizationId and projectId foreign keys, ensuring knowledge chunks are isolated per organization and optionally scoped to specific projects. This aligns with the existing data model where Organization contains Teams and Projects.

Source tracking provides full lineage for each knowledge chunk through multiple dimensions. The sourceType field categorizes chunks by their origin: transformation_session (from P2-05 variable qualification), general_manager (from initial context analysis), agent_analysis (from specialized expert outputs), domain_synthesis (from domain-level meta-analysis), or final_report (from final strategic synthesis). The sourceId field stores the UUID of the originating entity, while optional agentType (chaos_theory, fractals, non_linearity, interconnection, etc.) and domain (design_dependances, experience_identite, flux_valeur_strategie, people_croissance, structure_gouvernance) fields enable filtering by analysis specialty and strategic domain.

Content organization uses sectionType to categorize chunk semantics (resume_executif for executive summaries, risques for risk matrices, recommandations for strategic recommendations, contexte for context sections, etc.), with raw text stored in the content field and a contentHash field enabling deduplication to prevent storing identical chunks multiple times.

The embedding field integrates Supabase pgvector for semantic similarity search, defined as Unsupported("vector(768)") to accommodate the 768-dimensional output from Google's Gemini text-embedding-004 model. The flexible metadata JSON field stores additional analysis-specific data, while tokensCount tracks token consumption per chunk for usage monitoring.

Database indexes on organizationId, projectId, sourceType, domain, and agentType optimize query performance for common access patterns: filtering by tenant, scoping to projects, retrieving specific analysis types, domain-focused queries, and agent-specific searches.

A critical technical constraint was identified: Prisma ORM does not natively support PostgreSQL pgvector extension. The implementation requires a three-part workaround: (1) declare the embedding field as Unsupported("vector(768)") in the Prisma schema to prevent validation errors, (2) create the pgvector extension and vector similarity indexes using raw SQL migrations outside Prisma's migration system, and (3) bypass Prisma for vector operations by using the Supabase client directly for embedding storage and similarity searches.

This schema establishes the foundation for RAG-powered features including semantic search across past analyses, context retrieval for new analysis sessions, similarity detection across different projects, and intelligent recommendation of relevant historical insights based on current transformation context.

# RAG Knowledge Base API Endpoints and Use Cases Defined

Five priority RAG use cases identified with corresponding API endpoints for semantic search, contextual retrieval, and agent enrichment

During sequential thinking analysis (thought 4 of 8), the session defined a comprehensive RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) knowledge base architecture with five priority use cases and corresponding API endpoints for the transfo-ia-okr platform.

The first use case addresses simple semantic search where users submit natural language queries to receive top-K relevant chunks with similarity scores through POST /api/knowledge/search. This provides the foundation for knowledge retrieval across the platform.

The second use case enables contextual project search by accepting a query plus project_id parameter to filter chunks specific to individual projects. This allows users to ask project-scoped questions like "Quels risques ont été identifiés pour ce projet?" (What risks were identified for this project?) and receive focused results from that project's knowledge base.

The third use case implements cross-project organization-level search using organization_id to identify recurring patterns across multiple projects. This enables queries like "Quels sont les risques les plus fréquents dans notre organisation?" (What are the most frequent risks in our organization?) to surface organizational trends and common challenges.

The fourth use case provides agent enrichment by retrieving similar past analyses to enhance current analysis context. The General Manager agent specifically leverages this capability to incorporate historical knowledge when conducting new systemic analyses, improving quality through learned patterns from previous transformations.

The fifth use case delivers variable suggestions by analyzing current transformation variables against historical data to recommend complementary variables. This feature, mentioned as future functionality by the user, helps users discover relevant variables they might not have considered based on successful past analyses.

Five API endpoints support these use cases: POST /api/knowledge/search handles semantic search queries, POST /api/knowledge/similar finds analyses with similar characteristics, GET /api/knowledge/stats provides knowledge base metrics and statistics, POST /api/knowledge/index enables manual content indexing for administrators, and POST /api/knowledge/reindex triggers full reindexing of a project's content for administrators.

This RAG architecture positions the knowledge base as both a user-facing search tool and an agent-enhancement system, allowing the multi-agent orchestration system to learn from organizational history while helping users discover insights across their transformation portfolio.

# P3 RAG Preparation Pipeline Defined with Automatic Indexation and Event-Driven Architecture

Sequential thinking mapped RAG indexation pipeline requiring P3-00 task for event system, metadata standards, and structured agent outputs preparation

Sequential thinking analysis defined the complete RAG preparation pipeline architecture required to support Phase 4 knowledge retrieval capabilities, identifying critical Phase 3 preparation requirements.

The indexation pipeline follows a four-stage event-driven architecture. Stage 1 begins when any P3 agent completes analysis and emits an "agent_analysis_completed" event containing the analysis output. Stage 2 activates the Chunking Service which parses the JSON-structured agent output, segments content into chunks according to section_type classification (such as resume_executif, risques, recommandations), and calculates a content_hash for each chunk to enable deduplication of identical content across multiple analyses.

Stage 3 invokes the Embedding Service which calls the Gemini text-embedding-004 API to generate vector embeddings for semantic search. The service implements batch processing with maximum 100 chunks per API call to optimize throughput and cost efficiency. Stage 4 persists chunked content with embeddings to the KnowledgeChunk database table, triggering automatic vector index updates to maintain search performance as the knowledge base grows.

This pipeline architecture imposes three critical requirements on Phase 3 implementation. First, all 39 agent outputs must follow uniform structured formats with clearly identifiable sections enabling reliable parsing and chunking. Standardized section types like resume_executif (executive summary), risques (risks), and recommandations (recommendations) ensure consistent knowledge organization across diverse expert domains.

Second, P3 must implement a comprehensive event system emitting events at each workflow stage (agent start, agent completion, domain synthesis start, domain synthesis completion, chief reporter synthesis completion). These events enable decoupled, asynchronous triggering of indexation processes without tight coupling between analysis generation and knowledge storage.

Third, every agent output must carry consistent metadata including project_id for project-level knowledge scoping, org_id for multi-tenant isolation, domain for filtering by thematic area (Design/Dependencies, Experience/Identity, etc.), and agent_type for tracking knowledge source and expertise domain. This metadata enables contextual retrieval where RAG queries can filter by project, organization, domain, or specific expert perspectives.

To address these requirements, a new task P3-00 "Préparation structure pour RAG (event system, metadata standards)" must precede other P3 implementation tasks, establishing the foundational event architecture and output structure contracts before agent integration begins.

Cost analysis shows embedding generation represents negligible incremental expense. At $0.00001 per 1,000 tokens using Gemini text-embedding-004, a typical 150KB analysis (~40,000 tokens) costs approximately $0.0004 for embedding. This is 50-125x cheaper than the $0.02-0.05 cost of the 40 Gemini Flash inference calls required to generate the analysis content itself, making RAG indexation economically viable for all analyses without quota implications.

This RAG preparation within P3 creates a smooth path to P4 deployment by ensuring all knowledge generated through systemic analyses automatically feeds into the retrieval system without retroactive data migration or reformatting requirements.

# Phase 4 RAG System Architecture Finalized with Risk Mitigation and 14-Task Implementation Plan

Sequential thinking analysis completed identifying Supabase pgvector foundation, multi-tenant architecture, chunking strategy, and P3 preparation requirements with marginal cost at $0.0004 per analysis

The sequential thinking analysis concluded with thought 8 of 8, synthesizing a comprehensive Phase 4 RAG system architecture with risk assessment, mitigation strategies, and implementation roadmap. The analysis identified 14 granular tasks spanning database infrastructure, embedding pipeline, search APIs, and user interface components.

The technical foundation leverages Supabase's native pgvector extension rather than attempting vector operations through Prisma ORM, which lacks native vector type support. This architectural choice requires maintaining dual data access patterns: Prisma for standard relational operations and direct Supabase client for vector similarity searches. The trade-off accepts tooling fragmentation in exchange for mature vector search capabilities without additional infrastructure.

Five key risks were identified with corresponding mitigation strategies. The Prisma limitation risk is addressed through direct Supabase client usage for vector operations. Volume-related performance degradation is mitigated through org_id-based partitioning and historical data purging policies. Embedding quality risks from poor chunking are addressed through exhaustive testing and iterative tuning. Cumulative embedding costs, while marginal at $0.0004 per analysis using Google Gemini's text-embedding-004 model, require monitoring and budget alerting systems. The cold start problem, where an empty RAG system provides minimal value, could be mitigated by pre-populating with demonstration analyses.

The architecture enforces strict multi-tenant isolation with all queries filtered by org_id and protected through Row Level Security policies on pgvector tables. A soft delete pattern marks chunks as archived rather than removing them, preserving historical context and enabling potential reactivation. The versioning consideration raises the question of whether historical agent outputs should be reindexed when agent logic evolves, trading consistency against reprocessing costs.

Performance optimization includes caching frequent searches using Redis or Supabase's built-in cache, reducing redundant vector similarity computations. Data lifecycle management through partitioning and purging prevents index bloat as organizations accumulate analyses over time.

The analysis identified a critical dependency on Phase 3, requiring a new preparatory task P3-00 titled "Préparation RAG-ready" to establish foundational infrastructure. This task must implement an event system for capturing analysis outputs and define metadata standards ensuring uniform structure across all 32+ agent outputs. Without this standardization, consistent indexing and retrieval becomes problematic.

The UI implementation follows progressive enhancement principles, prioritizing search functionality that delivers immediate value before building the more complex conversational assistant interface. This staged rollout validates the retrieval system's effectiveness before layering on natural language interaction.

The synthesis concludes that Phase 4 represents a high-value, marginal-cost addition to the platform. User requested RAG system index all confirmed OKR data plus text, PDF, PPT, Excel, and image inputs beyond just agent analyses

User provided critical feedback on the proposed Phase 4 RAG Knowledge System architecture, significantly expanding the scope of data sources beyond the initially proposed agent-generated analyses.

The original P4 proposal defined two primary data sources: P2-05 transformation session variables and P3 multi-agent analysis outputs (General Manager reports, expert agent analyses, domain synthesizers). User feedback revealed this scope was too narrow and missed the core value proposition of organizational knowledge capture.

User requested the RAG system index the complete OKR database including all objectives, key results, initiatives, check-ins, comments, team structures, and organization information that users have confirmed, validated, and integrated into the application. This represents the actual operational data of the OKR platform—the validated strategic content that organizations are actively managing.

Additionally, user specified that all input documents and media provided throughout project lifecycles must be indexed. This includes transformation context variables collected during P2-05 sessions, plus text documents, PDF files uploaded for analysis, PowerPoint presentations, Excel spreadsheets with data, and images. These multi-format inputs represent the raw contextual information that feeds into strategic decision-making and should be searchable alongside structured OKR data and agent-generated insights.

This expanded scope transforms the RAG system from a repository of AI-generated analyses into a comprehensive organizational knowledge base that bridges structured operational data (OKRs), unstructured input documents (PDFs, presentations, spreadsheets, images), and AI-generated strategic insights (agent analyses). The system would enable queries like "show me all OKRs related to this transformation context" or "find initiatives similar to this uploaded document" or "what risks were identified across all projects in this domain."

User also raised a fundamental architectural question: why was LangGraph not chosen as the initial architectural foundation for the multi-agent orchestration system? This question suggests user familiarity with LangGraph as a framework specifically designed for building stateful multi-agent applications with complex workflows, and questions whether building custom orchestration logic (as proposed in P3) represents reinventing capabilities that LangGraph provides out-of-the-box.

The LangGraph question has significant architectural implications. LangGraph offers built-in support for agent graphs, state management, conditional edges, human-in-the-loop patterns, persistence, and streaming—capabilities that would need to be custom-built in the proposed P3 architecture. However, the decision to not use LangGraph initially may relate to factors like framework complexity, dependency management, team expertise, or desire for fine-grained control over orchestration logic.

This feedback indicates the RAG system architecture requires substantial revision to accommodate diverse data sources with different formats, extraction requirements, and chunking strategies. PDFs and presentations need OCR or text extraction, Excel files need structured data parsing, images need vision model processing or metadata extraction, and OKR database content needs transformation from relational structures to searchable chunks with preserved relationships.

# Hybrid Architecture Validated: Custom P2-05 with LangGraph-Based P3/P4

User approved hybrid approach preserving working P2-05 custom implementation while adopting LangGraph framework for P3/P4 orchestration and RAG capabilities

The user validated the hybrid architectural approach (Option C) for the transfo-ia-okr platform's Phase 3 and Phase 4 development, establishing a clear division between existing and future system components.

The approved architecture maintains three distinct layers: P2-05 transformation agent preserves its current custom implementation built on Next.js API routes with direct Gemini SDK calls and manual orchestration, P3 systemic analysis (39-agent orchestration) and P4 RAG functionality adopt LangGraph as their foundation framework, and an API interface layer connects the custom P2-05 system with the LangGraph-based P3/P4 subsystem.

The decision rationale centers on pragmatic effort optimization and risk management. The P2-05 conversational agent for variable transformation already functions correctly with its custom TypeScript orchestration, streaming architecture, and database persistence. Migrating this working system to LangGraph would introduce unnecessary risk and development effort without proportional benefit. Conversely, P3's 39-agent parallel orchestration with complex state management and P4's RAG semantic search requirements align precisely with LangGraph's core capabilities, making the framework adoption highly cost-effective for these features.

The user articulated an architectural coherence principle: "Ce qui fonctionne fonctionne et ce qui reste à bâtir a besoin d'un socle nouveau" (What works continues working, and what remains to be built needs a new foundation). This principle acknowledges that P2-05's simple single-agent conversational pattern justified custom implementation, while P3/P4's enterprise-grade multi-agent orchestration, parallel execution, state machines, and RAG integration justify framework adoption to avoid reinventing complex orchestration primitives.

The hybrid approach introduces architectural heterogeneity but provides clear separation of concerns. P2-05 handles user-facing transformation variable collection through conversational UI, outputting structured transformation context. P3/P4 consume this context via API, orchestrate deep multi-agent systemic analysis using LangGraph's graph execution engine, and provide RAG-powered semantic search across historical analyses. # Hybrid Architecture with Python LangGraph Microservice for P3/P4

Architecture redesigned to use Python LangGraph with FastAPI microservice for agent orchestration and RAG while maintaining existing Next.js TypeScript frontend

A major architectural decision was made during sequential thinking analysis (thought 1 of 6) to adopt a hybrid architecture combining the existing Next.js TypeScript stack with a new Python LangGraph microservice for advanced agent orchestration and RAG capabilities.

The architecture splits the system into two primary layers. The existing TypeScript layer continues handling the Next.js frontend with dashboard OKR management, P2-05 chat agent, knowledge search UI, along with Supabase authentication, OKR CRUD operations, and team/user management. This preserves all Phase 1 and Phase 2 functionality without migration risk.

The new Python layer introduces LangGraph for implementing P3's 39-agent orchestration system, P4's RAG knowledge retrieval, and document ingestion pipelines. Python was selected over LangGraph.js specifically because the Python LangGraph ecosystem offers greater maturity with more stable tooling, broader community support, and richer integration libraries for advanced agent workflows.

The Python components are exposed as a microservice using FastAPI, providing RESTful endpoints that the Next.js frontend consumes. This microservice architecture enables independent scaling, allows the LangGraph service to leverage Python's rich AI/ML ecosystem, and maintains clean separation between the conversational UI layer and the complex multi-agent orchestration layer.

Both services share a single Supabase PostgreSQL database, ensuring data consistency across the hybrid stack. The existing Prisma-managed tables remain unchanged, while new tables are added to store P3 systemic analysis results (SystemicAnalysis, DomainAnalysis, AgentAnalysis entities). The database is extended with pgvector extension to support vector embeddings for P4 RAG semantic search, while Supabase Storage provides document persistence for the ingestion pipeline.

The P2-05 conversational transformation agent, already implemented in TypeScript with streaming chat capabilities, remains in the Next.js layer but gains the ability to trigger P3 multi-agent analyses by making HTTP calls to the FastAPI endpoints. This preserves the seamless UX flow where users complete variable qualification in P2-05, then optionally launch comprehensive systemic analysis powered by the Python LangGraph orchestration.

This hybrid approach balances pragmatism with capability: leveraging Next.js TypeScript strengths for UI and CRUD while adopting Python LangGraph for advanced agent coordination where ecosystem maturity matters most. The shared database and REST API boundary provide clean integration points with independent deployment and scaling characteristics for each service.

# Python LangGraph Microservice Architecture Defined for P3 and P4 Implementation

Separate langgraph-service microservice planned with FastAPI, LangGraph workflows, 39 domain-organized agents, RAG pipeline, and Supabase integration

Sequential thinking analysis defined a comprehensive Python microservice architecture using LangGraph to implement Phase 3 systemic analysis and Phase 4 RAG capabilities separate from the existing Next.js application.

The architecture introduces a new langgraph-service/ directory at project root containing a complete Python application with its own dependency management (pyproject.toml using uv or poetry), environment configuration (.env for GEMINI_API_KEY, SUPABASE_URL, etc.), and containerization (Dockerfile for deployment). This separation isolates the complex agent orchestration logic from the Next.js frontend while enabling independent scaling and deployment.

The application structure follows FastAPI patterns with app/main.py as the entry point and app/config.py for settings management. The database layer in app/db/ provides a Supabase client (supabase.py) and SQLAlchemy models (models.py) that mirror the existing Prisma schema, ensuring data model consistency between Next.js and Python services while leveraging SQLAlchemy's ORM capabilities for complex queries and pgvector integration.

The agent layer in app/agents/ organizes the 39 specialized experts hierarchically. The general_manager.py file implements the orchestration coordinator, while five domain subdirectories (design_dependances/, experience_identite/, flux_valeur_strategie/, people_croissance/, structure_gouvernance/) contain individual agent implementations (chaos_theory.py, fractals.py, holism.py, emergence.py, etc.) plus a synthesizer.py module for each domain that aggregates expert outputs. The rapporteur_chef.py module at the root level implements the Chief Reporter synthesis across all selected domains.

LangGraph workflow definitions reside in app/graphs/. The systemic_analysis.py module defines the P3 multi-agent orchestration graph with conditional routing (single domain terminates at domain expert, multiple domains route to Chief Reporter), parallelism constraints (max 5 concurrent domains), and state management for streaming progress. The rag_pipeline.py module defines the P4 knowledge retrieval workflow including query understanding, retrieval, reranking, and answer generation.

The RAG subsystem in app/rag/ implements four core capabilities. The embeddings.py module wraps Gemini text-embedding-004 API for vector generation. The chunking.py module implements content splitting strategies by section_type with content_hash calculation for deduplication. The retriever.py module provides pgvector-backed semantic search with metadata filtering (project_id, org_id, domain, agent_type). The ingestion.py module uses the Unstructured library to parse uploaded documents (PDF, DOCX, PPTX) for knowledge base expansion.

Agent prompts migrate from the N8N JSON workflow format to individual YAML files in app/prompts/, enabling version control, easier editing, and programmatic loading. This addresses the database storage decision while maintaining prompt configurability through file-based updates deployed with the service.

The API layer in app/api/routes/ exposes three endpoint groups. The analysis.py module provides POST /analysis/start to initiate systemic analyses with domain selection and GET /analysis/{id} to retrieve analysis status and results. The knowledge.py module provides POST /knowledge/search for semantic search queries against the RAG knowledge base with optional filtering. The documents.py module provides POST /documents/upload for ingesting user documents into the knowledge base. All endpoints use Pydantic schemas from app/api/schemas.py for request validation and response serialization.

The technology stack combines LangGraph and LangChain for agent orchestration and workflow management, FastAPI for high-performance REST APIs and WebSocket streaming, SQLAlchemy for database access with pgvector extension support, Supabase Python client for authentication and real-time subscriptions, google-generativeai SDK for Gemini API access, and Unstructured library for multi-format document parsing.

A comprehensive test suite in tests/ covers agent behavior (test_agents.py), workflow orchestration (test_graphs.py), and RAG functionality (test_rag.py), ensuring reliability as the system evolves.

This microservice architecture enables independent scaling of compute-intensive agent processing separate from the Next.js frontend, leverages Python's rich AI/ML ecosystem (LangChain, Unstructured, pgvector), and positions the platform for future enhancements like additional agent types, alternative LLM providers, or advanced RAG techniques without impacting the core Next.js application.

# LangGraph Workflow Architecture Designed for P3 Multi-Agent Strategic Analysis Orchestration

Sequential thinking defines Python LangGraph implementation with parallel domain execution, conditional Chief Reporter routing, and sub-graph structures for 39-agent orchestration

Sequential thinking MCP server processing thought 3 of 6 defined the LangGraph workflow architecture for Phase 3 strategic analysis orchestration. The design implements a Python-based state graph managing the execution of 39 specialized agents across 5 strategic domains with conditional reporting logic.

The core AnalysisState TypedDict structure captures the complete analysis lifecycle: input parameters include project_id, transformation_variables from P2-05, and selected_domains list; progress tracking maintains general_manager_output, domain_outputs dictionary keyed by domain name, and agent_outputs dictionary keyed by agent name; final state includes rapport_final and status field with values pending/running/completed/failed.

The main StateGraph orchestrates high-level workflow through seven node types. The general_manager node receives transformation variables and determines analysis scope. The domain_router node dispatches to selected domains based on General Manager recommendations. Five domain nodes (design_dependances for Design & Dependencies, experience_identite for Experience & Identity, flux_valeur_strategie for Value Flow & Strategy, people_croissance for People & Growth, structure_gouvernance for Structure & Governance) execute domain-specific analysis. The aggregator node collects all domain outputs. The rapporteur_chef node synthesizes cross-domain insights when two or more domains are selected.

Edge configuration implements the conditional logic: general_manager connects directly to domain_router, which uses conditional edges with route_to_selected_domains function to dynamically route to activated domains, all domain nodes converge on aggregator, and aggregator uses should_call_rapporteur conditional to either invoke rapporteur_chef (when N≥2 domains) or proceed directly to END.

Each domain implements a sub-graph pattern maintaining consistent structure across the five domains. Using Design & Dependencies as the example: the domain sub-graph instantiates nodes for all eight agents (chaos_theory, fractals, network_theory, plus five others), connects START edge to all agents enabling parallel execution, routes all agent outputs to a synthesizer node, and connects synthesizer to END. This pattern repeats for each domain with its specific agent set.

LangGraph framework provides five critical capabilities for this architecture: native parallel execution runs all five domains simultaneously and all agents within each domain concurrently, automatic state persistence maintains AnalysisState throughout execution without manual serialization, streaming updates deliver real-time progress via callback mechanisms, automatic retry logic handles transient failures in agent invocations, and checkpointing enables recovery from crashes by resuming from last successful state.

The Python pseudocode structure uses StateGraph class from langgraph.graph, defines nodes via add_node method accepting node names and handler functions, establishes edges through add_edge for direct connections and add_conditional_edges for routing logic with dictionary-based destination mapping, and leverages TypedDict for type-safe state management.

This architecture directly implements the N8N workflow structure previously analyzed (39 agents across 5 domains with General Manager orchestration and Chief Reporter synthesis) but translates it into a Python-based LangGraph implementation suitable for integration into the transfo-ia-okr Next.js application via API endpoints, enabling execution control, state monitoring, and result persistence within the existing Supabase PostgreSQL infrastructure.

Faits: ["LangGraph StateGraph defines AnalysisState with project_id, transformation_variables, selected_domains inputs, progress tracking via general_manager_output/domain_outputs/agent_outputs, and final rapport_final with status (pending/running/completed/failed)","Main graph nodes include general_manager, domain_router for dispatch, five domain nodes (design_dependances, experience_identite, flux_valeur_strategie, people_croissance, structure_gouvernance), aggregator for output collection, and rapporteur_chef for final synthesis","Conditional edges route from domain_router to selected domains, aggregate domain outputs, and conditionally invoke rapporteur_chef when N≥2 domains selected","Each domain implements sub-graph with parallel agent execution: domain-specific agents (8 agents for Design & Dependencies including chaos_theory, fractals, network_theory) feed into domain synthesizer node","LangGraph provides native parallel execution for 5 domains and agents within each domain, automatic state persistence, streaming updates via callbacks, automatic retry on failure, and checkpointing for crash recovery","Graph flow: general_manager → domain_router → parallel domain execution → aggregator → conditional rapporteur_chef → END","Domain sub-graph pattern: START → parallel agents → synthesizer → END for consistent domain processing structure"]
summary: LangGraph Workflow Architecture Designed for P3 Multi-Agent Strategic Analysis Orchestration

# Phase 4 RAG Architecture Expanded with LangGraph Pipelines and Multi-Source Document Ingestion

Sequential thinking defines comprehensive RAG system ingesting 10 source types through LangGraph orchestration with conditional routing and pgvector storage

The sequential thinking analysis (thought 4 of 6) expanded the Phase 4 RAG architecture to encompass comprehensive multi-source document ingestion orchestrated through LangGraph state machines with sophisticated parsing and storage strategies.

The data ingestion scope broadened to capture 10 distinct source types forming the complete knowledge base: direct database entities (OKRs including objectives/key results/initiatives, check-ins with progression tracking and comments, transformation variables from P2-05 sessions, conversational chat messages from P2-05 interactions, and systemic analysis outputs from P3's 39 agents), uploaded documents requiring parsing (PDF documents via Unstructured library with semantic chunking, PowerPoint presentations parsed slide-by-slide, Excel spreadsheets processed with Pandas by sheet or table), images processed through Gemini Vision OCR for diagram and photo text extraction, and user-generated comments attached to any system object.

The LangGraph ingestion pipeline implements a StateGraph pattern with conditional routing architecture. The flow begins with a classifier node determining document type, then routes to specialized parser nodes (parse_pdf, parse_ppt, parse_excel, parse_image_ocr, parse_db_entity) based on classification results. All parsers converge to a semantic chunking node that segments content intelligently, followed by an embedder node creating vector representations, concluding with storage in pgvector. The conditional routing enables extensibility - adding new document types requires only new parser nodes and routing rules without modifying the core pipeline structure.

The search pipeline StateGraph implements a four-stage retrieval-augmented generation flow: query_analyzer interprets user intent and extracts search parameters, retriever performs vector similarity search against pgvector, reranker re-scores results using more sophisticated relevance models, and generator produces contextual answers incorporating retrieved knowledge chunks. This separation of concerns enables independent optimization of each stage.

The knowledge_chunks table schema evolved to support multi-tenant, multi-source ingestion with comprehensive metadata. Organization_id with RLS policies ensures tenant isolation. Source tracking fields (source_type, source_id, source_subtype) maintain lineage for each chunk back to its origin - whether an OKR objective, a chaos theory analysis section, or a PDF page. Content hash enables deduplication preventing redundant embeddings. The metadata JSONB field provides flexible storage for source-specific attributes. File metadata (file_name, page_number) supports document-oriented search. The embedding column uses vector(768) matching Gemini text-embedding-004's dimensionality.

Vector search optimization uses HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) indexing with cosine similarity operations, providing logarithmic search complexity for high-dimensional vector spaces. Additional B-tree indexes on organization_id and source_type accelerate filtered queries combining vector similarity with tenant or source constraints.

The architecture supports section-type categorization (resume, risque, recommandation) enabling users to filter search results by content category - for example, retrieving only risk assessments or recommendations from historical analyses. This structured approach transforms raw analysis outputs into queryable knowledge.

The Python-based LangGraph implementation provides visual pipeline inspection, checkpoint-based recovery for long-running ingestion jobs, and programmatic pipeline composition enabling dynamic workflow construction based on document characteristics. This positions the RAG system as a flexible knowledge processing engine adaptable to evolving document types and analysis needs.

Faits: ["RAG system ingests 10 data source types: OKRs, check-ins, P2-05 transformation variables, P2-05 chat conversations, P3 systemic analyses, uploaded PDFs, PowerPoint presentations, Excel spreadsheets, images with OCR, and comments","LangGraph ingestion pipeline implements StateGraph with nodes for classification, parsing (PDF/PPT/Excel/Image/DB), semantic chunking, embedding, and pgvector storage","Conditional routing in ingestion graph dispatches documents to appropriate parser based on classifier output (pdf/ppt/excel/image/db_entity)","Search pipeline implements StateGraph with query analysis, pgvector retrieval, reranking, and context-aware answer generation nodes","Document parsing uses Unstructured library for PDFs with semantic chunking, Unstructured for PowerPoint by slide, Pandas for Excel by sheet/table, and Gemini Vision for image OCR","knowledge_chunks table schema includes organization_id with RLS, project_id reference, source tracking (source_type, source_id, source_subtype), content with hash for deduplication, metadata JSONB, file metadata (name, page_number), and vector(768) embedding field","Vector index uses HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) with cosine similarity operations for efficient similarity search","Additional indexes created on organization_id and source_type columns for filtering performance","Source types enumerated: okr, checkin, transformation, analysis, document, comment with subtypes like objective, key_result, pdf, chaos_theory","Section types categorized as resume, risque, recommandation for structured content organization"]

# Phase 3 Architecture Defined - Python Microservice with LangGraph Multi-Agent Orchestration and 22 Implementation Tasks

Sequential thinking establishes Python FastAPI microservice architecture using LangGraph for 39-agent orchestration with real-time streaming, domain visualization, and quota management

The sequential thinking analysis reached thought 5 of 6, delivering a comprehensive 22-task implementation plan for Phase 3 that fundamentally establishes a Python microservice architecture for multi-agent strategic analysis. This represents a significant architectural decision to complement the Next.js application with a dedicated Python backend specialized for AI agent orchestration.

The foundation layer (P3-00 through P3-04) establishes the Python microservice infrastructure. Task P3-00 creates the project structure with pyproject.toml for dependency management, FastAPI as the web framework, configuration management, and Dockerfile for containerized deployment. This microservice operates independently from the Next.js application, communicating via REST and WebSocket APIs.

The data layer requires dual-ORM support. Task P3-01 defines Prisma schema additions for three new tables: SystemicAnalysis captures overall analysis metadata, DomainAnalysis stores outputs from the five domain synthesizers, and AgentAnalysis persists individual agent results. Migration SQL enables Supabase schema evolution. Task P3-02 creates SQLAlchemy models mirroring these Prisma tables, enabling the Python microservice to read transformation session inputs and write analysis outputs to the shared PostgreSQL database.

The agent implementation strategy migrates N8N's 39 agent prompts to a more maintainable format. Task P3-03 extracts prompts from the N8N JSON workflow into individual YAML files, enabling version control, optimization, and easier iteration. Task P3-04 implements a Python base class abstracting common agent operations: loading prompts from YAML, invoking Google Gemini API, and parsing structured outputs into consistent formats.

Agent implementation distributes across five domain-specific tasks matching N8N's organizational structure. P3-05 implements the Design & Dependencies domain with 8 agents covering Chaos Theory, Dynamic Complexity, Edge of Chaos, Fractals, Interconnectedness, Network Theory, Nonlinearity, and Systems Mapping plus a domain synthesizer. P3-06 implements Experience & Identity with 5 agents for Holism, Emergence, Adaptation, Mental Models, and Self-Organization. P3-07 implements Value Flow & Strategy with 6 agents covering Causal Loop Diagrams, Feedback Loops, Leverage Points, System Dynamics, Systemic Intervention, and Unintended Consequences. P3-08 implements People & Growth with 8 agents for Agent-Based Modeling, Attractors, Fitness Landscapes, Phase Transitions, Power Laws, Resilience, Scaling, and Self-Organized Criticality. P3-09 implements Structure & Governance with 5 agents covering Boundaries, Hierarchies, System Archetypes, Systems, and Viable System Model.

Two critical orchestration agents receive dedicated implementation focus. Task P3-10 implements the General Manager agent responsible for initial analysis orchestration and routing qualified transformation variables to appropriate domain workflows. Task P3-11 implements the Chief Reporter agent synthesizing outputs from all five domain synthesizers into a cohesive final strategic report.

The core orchestration engine comes in task P3-12, implementing the complete LangGraph workflow with sophisticated features including intelligent routing between agents, parallel execution of domain-specific workflows, and comprehensive state management tracking execution progress and intermediate results across 39+ agents.

The API layer provides three distinct interaction patterns. Task P3-13 creates POST /analysis/start accepting transformation session context and triggering asynchronous graph execution. Task P3-14 implements WebSocket /analysis/{id}/stream delivering real-time progress updates as agents complete, enabling responsive UI updates during multi-minute analysis runs. Task P3-15 provides REST endpoints for polling status and retrieving complete or partial results by analysis ID or specific domain.

Integration with the Next.js application happens through task P3-16, creating a TypeScript service layer wrapping FastAPI endpoints with type-safe interfaces for starting analyses, subscribing to streaming updates, and fetching results.

The user interface implementation follows progressive disclosure principles. Task P3-17 creates a domain selection page allowing users to customize which domains participate in analysis, potentially reducing cost and latency for focused investigations. Task P3-18 implements real-time streaming visualization displaying agent progress and intermediate results as they arrive via WebSocket. Task P3-19 builds comprehensive result visualization supporting navigation by domain, drilling into individual agent outputs, and displaying the final synthesized report.

Access control is enforced through task P3-20, implementing quota management limiting normal users to 2 analysis runs per project while granting unlimited access to superadmin roles. This prevents resource abuse while demonstrating value to trial users before requiring upgrades.

Quality assurance in task P3-21 spans three testing layers: unit tests validating individual agent behavior and output structure, graph tests verifying orchestration logic and state transitions, and end-to-end tests confirming the complete pipeline from API call through database persistence to UI rendering.

Five architectural risks were assessed with mitigation strategies. Prisma's lack of native vector support is resolved through direct Supabase client usage for vector operations. Index performance degradation under volume is addressed through org_id partitioning and data lifecycle policies. Embedding quality risks require exhaustive chunking tests and iterative tuning. Embedding costs, though low at $0.0004 per analysis, require monitoring infrastructure. The cold start problem where empty RAG systems provide minimal value could be mitigated through demo data pre-population.

Key architectural considerations include strict multi-tenant RLS enforcement on all vector queries, soft delete patterns preserving historical data, versioning strategies for reindexing when agent logic changes, and caching layers for frequent searches using Redis or Supabase cache.
